units.la: MDLXXVI
Τὰ πρὸ τῶν κατηγοριῶν.
units.tr: Of the things before the categories.

units.la: CVR CATEGORIAE CAETERIS libris Dialecticis, & Categoriis τὰ πρὸ τῶν κατηγορίας ὧν praponantur: quae vero τὰ μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας dicuntur, Categoriis subiiciantur.
units.tr: The things which are placed before the Categories, in the other Dialectical books, are to be put before the Categories; but those which are called the things after the Categories are to be subjoined to the Categories.

units.la: QVI Categorias praetermittunt, carceribus neglectis, metam frustra dicunt se attigisse. Quod autē Categoriae sint carceres Διαλεκτικῆς φραγματείας eruditi omnes norunt. Nam ex lege κῇ? πάντος, ὡς ἐν γεϱμμῇ σιγμὴ καὶ ἐν τειγώνῳ γεϱμμὴ: sic in propositione ὅρoι, & propositiones in syllogismo. Ex qua etiā lege, ordo cōmentariorū & ὑποκειμένων intelligitur. Sed nō omnia quae antecedunt, necessario sunt pertractanda. Sic enim ab ipso uno (quod dicitur) incipere liceat. Quare regula τὸ καθ' αὑτὸ adhibenda est, qua necessitate huius primae omnium tractationis metiamur. De necessitate non licet dubitare per primum modum τὸ καθ' αὑτὸ: primus .n. modus τὸ καθ' αὑτὸ est: ὅιον τριγώνῳ γεϱμμὴ, καὶ γεϱμμῇ σιγμή. Haec est τάξις ς καὶ ἀνάγκη.
units.tr: Those who omit the Categories, having neglected the starting-posts, say in vain that they have reached the goal. That the Categories are the starting-posts of the Dialectical discipline all the learned know. For by the law of "in every case," as a point is in a line and a line in a triangle, so are the terms in a proposition, and the propositions in a syllogism. By this same law the order of the commentaries and of the subjects is understood. But not everything that precedes must necessarily be treated; for thus one might begin from the "one itself," as they say. Therefore the rule of "per se" must be applied, by which we measure the necessity of this first of all treatments. Concerning necessity there is no room for doubt according to the first mode of "per se": for the first mode of "per se" is such as "a line in a triangle" and "a point in a line." This is the order and the necessity.

units.la: Neq; sūt æqui iudices, qui Categorias Dialectico se detrahere pronunciāt, ut summo Philosopho restituāt. Ad ipsū metaphysicū prouocamus:qui docet se nō tractare Categorias vt Ca-tegorias (hoc enim Dialectici esse) & neg bit quarto libro summæ Philosophiæ, tradit Catego-rias: quum τὰ πολλαχῶς λεγόμενα in illo libro explicentur: quorum distincta notitia in consideratione ὄντος ἢ οὐσίας est summopere necessaria.
units.tr: Nor are they fair judges who pronounce that the Categories are withdrawn from the Dialectician, in order to restore them to the highest Philosopher. We appeal to the Metaphysician himself, who teaches that he does not treat the Categories as Categories (for this belongs to the Dialecticians), and in the fourth book of his Summa of Philosophy he hands down the Categories, since the things said in many ways are explained in that book, whose distinct knowledge is exceedingly necessary for the consideration of being or substance.

units.la: Tanti autem momenti sunt Categoriæ, vt non nisi his tanquam fundamentis primo rite ac fideque iactis, cætera recte superstrui possint. Neque enim recte definire οὐσίας possis; neque accidentia, accidentiumque genera recte distinguere in propositionibus, & syllogismis μὴ ἀποδεικτικῶς [?] Categoriarum doctrinam.
units.tr: The Categories are of such weight that unless they are first laid rightly and faithfully as foundations, the rest cannot be built properly upon them. For you could neither rightly define substance, nor rightly distinguish accidents and the kinds of accidents in propositions and syllogisms, without the doctrine of the Categories, not demonstratively [?].

units.la: Vt autem Categoriæ & genera ipsa inter se distinguuntur, necessario velut προδιορισμοὶ quædam fuerunt præscribendi & præponendi: quorum ea est ratio, vt antecedens sequente latius pateat, & sit γνωστότερος: & sic deinceps, eousque dum decem Categoriæ distinctæ constituantur.
units.tr: Now, so that the Categories and the genera themselves may be distinguished from one another, certain preliminary delimitations had necessarily to be prescribed and placed in front, the reason for which is that the antecedent should extend more widely than the sequent and be more known; and so on, until the ten distinct Categories are established.

units.la: Cæterum quot sunt Categoriarum summa genera: tot sunt etiam veluti ὑποκείμενα γένη, quorum proprietates & πάθη quædam in singulis Categoriis traduntur. Hinc etiam ὑπαγωγή est, CATEGORIAE, non Categoriæ. Decem Categoriis subnectuntur τὰ μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας: quia nimirum Categorias ita sequuntur, vt alicui generi separatim non sint addita, quia nimirum sunt communia quædam ἐπόμενα [?].
units.tr: Moreover, as many as there are the highest genera of the Categories, so many are also, as it were, underlying genera, whose properties and certain affections are handed down in the individual Categories. Hence also the subordination is "CATEGORIAE," not "Categoriae." The things after the Categories are subjoined to the ten Categories: because, of course, they follow the Categories in such a way that they are not added separately to any one genus, since they are certain common consequences [?].

units.la: Primus prodiorismus est, de homonymis: qui est γενικώτατος reliquorum, & tāquam initium distinguendi categorias. Nam non distinctis homonymis, frustra genera constituere conaberis.
units.tr: The first preliminary delimitation concerns homonyms, which is the most general of the rest, and as it were the beginning of distinguishing the categories. For unless the homonyms are distinguished, you will attempt in vain to constitute the genera.

units.la: Homonyma inquit Aristotelcs, dicuntur illa quorum nomē solum est commune:sed ratio es-sentiæ seu definitio secundū nomen illud com-mune, non est eadem: ut homo vivus, & picta hominis figura, dicuntur homo ὁμωνύμως. Nam si definiantur, picta hominis figura, non poterit dici animal: neque definitio hominis, qua est animal, ei convenet.
units.tr: Aristotle says: homonyms are those things of which the name alone is common, but the account of the essence, or the definition according to that common name, is not the same; as a living man and a painted figure of a man are said to be "man" homonymously. For if the painted figure of a man is defined, it cannot be called an animal; nor will the definition of man, which is "animal," apply to it.

units.la: Homonymiæ vero aut sunt ὑπὸ τύχης, cum nulla intercedit similitudo. Aut sunt propter similitudinem quandā, ut in metaphoris. Aut propter analogiam: ut videre, idem κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν dicitur mensis, & oculorum: ut enim oculi vident colores, ita mēs νοητὰ εἴδη. Aut quia unum prius dicitur, quàm alterum, i. κατὰ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον: ut ὄν dicitur prius de substantia, posterius de accidente: & Ecclesia dicitur primò de illo cœtu, qui accuratissimè retinet doctrinam Filii Dei. Qui verò cœtus minimè omnium doctrinam Filii Dei retinet, dicitur ἐγγὺς τῆς μὴ Ἐκκλη-σίας. Aut propter logicum aliquod genus, ut cùm febris definitur logicè, calor naturalis mutatus in igneū absque subiectis primis quæ sunt tria καθ᾽ ἕκαστα εἴδη, nempe spiritus, humores, & ipsa substantia. Ex his logicum genus dicitur ἐγγὺς τῷ γένει, & logicam categoriam constituit: quæ est veluti rudimentum nostræ notitiæ.
units.tr: Homonymies, indeed, are either by chance, when no resemblance intervenes; or on account of some likeness, as in metaphors; or on account of analogy, as "to see" is said analogically of the mind and of the eyes: for as the eyes see colours, so the mind sees intelligible forms. Or because one thing is said before another, that is, according to priority and posteriority: as "being" is said first of substance, afterwards of accident; and "Church" is said first of that assembly which most accurately retains the doctrine of the Son of God, while that assembly which by no means retains the doctrine of the Son of God is said to be "near to not-Church." Or on account of some logical genus, as when fever is defined logically as natural heat changed into fire without the primary subjects, which are the three particular kinds, namely spirits, humours, and the substance itself. From these, the logical genus is said to be "near the genus," and constitutes the logical category, which is as it were the rudiment of our knowledge.

units.la: Distin&ta Homonymia, elucescit συνώνυμος claráque rei notitia. Synonyma sunt quorum nomen commune est, & definitio secundum illud nomè, eadem est: ut homo & bos συνωνύμως dicuntur animal: & definitio animalis de utroque verè dicitur.
units.tr: With homonymy distinguished, synonymy emerges and the clear knowledge of the thing. Synonyms are those of which the name is common and the definition according to that name is the same; as man and ox are said synonymously to be animal, and the definition of animal is truly predicated of both.

units.la: Logicum genus propè accedit ad Synonymum. Iccirco etiam synonymum logicum[?] ἐγγὺς τῷ γένει dicitur. Remotius est quod κατὰ πρότερον & ὕστερον dicitur. Multo remotius quod καθ' ὁμοιότητα, καὶ κατ' ἀναλογίαν dicitur. Remotissimum & ut dicit Aristoteles, πολὺ ἀπέχον, τὸ ἀπὸ τύχης.
units.tr: The logical genus comes close to the synonym; therefore it is also called the logical synonym "near the genus." That which is said according to priority and posteriority is more remote. Much more remote is that which is said according to likeness and according to analogy. The most remote, and, as Aristotle says, "far removed," is that which is by chance.

units.la: Quæ non prædicatur συνωνύμως in quid, prædicantur παρωνύμως in quale. Dicuntur paro-nyma quæ discrepant em[?] casu denominationem ab aliquo acceperunt, ut à grammatica, grammaticus παρωνύμως dicitur: & à statua statuarius.
units.tr: Those things which are not predicated synonymously in what [quid], are predicated paronymously in what sort [quale]. Paronyms are those which differ in case and have received their denomination from something: as from grammar, the grammarian is called paronymously "grammarian"; and from a statue, the statuary.

units.la: In lib de interpretatione rectè stare dicuntur Aristoteli tertia persona præsentis, & quæ primum casum grammatici non rectè vocant, cum non sit casus sed rectum quid. Hic etiam rectè stare dicuntur abstracta accidentium à quibus denominantur παρωνύμως subiecta κατηγορικὰ[?] accidentium.
units.tr: In the book On Interpretation, the third person of the present is said by Aristotle to stand correctly, and what the grammarians do not rightly call the first case, since it is not a case but something upright. Here also the abstracts of accidents, from which the subjects of accidents are denominated paronymously, are said to stand correctly as categorical [?].

units.la: Verùm grammatici deducunt iustum à iustitia, cum tamen iustitia non sit ἀτώσις dialectico, ut qui iustum denominet à iustitia. Sic Aristoteles in categoria τῶν πρός τι, ἀνακεῖσθαι[?], ἢ ἔξ ἀναγ[?], ἢ καθῆσθαι[?], αὐτὰ μὲν ἃ εἰσὶ θέσεις, παρωνύμως δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν εἰρημένων θέσεων λέγονται. At grammaticus non dicet ἀνάκλισιν dici παρωνύμως, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀναιρέσεως[?]. Quo in loco notandum est licere etiam vocabula substituere: neque enim dixit ἀναλλίνεσθαι[?], sed ἀναιρεῖσθαι.
units.tr: Yet the grammarians derive "just" from "justice," although justice is not a predicate for the dialectician, as one who would denominate the just from justice. So Aristotle, in the category of relatives, says: "reclining, or having been held, or sitting," these themselves are positions, but they are said paronymously from the positions mentioned. But the grammarian will not say that "reclining" is said paronymously from the removal. In this place it must be noted that it is also permitted to substitute words: for he did not say "being reclined," but "being removed."

units.la: Et vt ὅ[?]ῳ[?] simplices inducendi in categorias, eximantur ex propositionibus & orationibus: dicendum est huc in modū. Quicquid dicitur, aut est complexum seu compositum, aut simplex &sine complexione, quam vocant. Complexa seu composita sunt illa, homo currit: homo vincit. Simplicia sunt & incomplexa, vt ita dicam, verba & nomina: vt homo, bos, currit, vincit.
units.tr: And so that the simple things may be brought into the categories, let them be taken out from propositions and sentences; it must be said in this manner. Whatever is said is either complex or composite, or simple and without complexion, as they call it. Complex or composite are those such as "man runs," "man conquers." Simple and uncomplex, so to speak, are words and nouns: such as "man," "ox," "runs," "conquers."

units.la: Distincta sunt vocabula omnia superioribusprodiorismis. Vt autem ad distinctionem cate-goriarum propiùs accedamus: quaenam sint fun-damenta, seu ὑποκείμενα notionum priorum,& eorum quae dicuntur de rebus seu de ipsis subiectis in quid, aut κατὰ πρωνύμως praedicantur, pro diorismo quodam exponere oportet. hic autem prodiorismus erit diuisio quaedam τῶν ὄντων, hûc in modû. Eorum quae sunt, quaedā καθ' ὑποκειμένῳ[?] dicuntur, in subiecto vero non insunt: vt homo dicitur de hoc homine, idque συνωνύμως[?]: in subiecto vero non inest: quia non praedicatur παρωνύμως de hoc homine. Quaedā vero sunt in subiecto, de subiecto vero non dicuntur, vt sunt accidentia καθ' ἕκαστα, & singularia ἀπλῶς vt grammatica in animo Donati. Sunt autem in subiecto haec accidetia singularia, non vt partes in toto. Nam si essent vt partes in toto, essent vt partes substantiarum, quod est absurdum.
units.tr: All the words have been distinguished by the preceding preliminary delimitations. But in order to come closer to the distinction of the categories, it is fitting to set out by a certain delimitation what are the foundations, or underlying things, of the prior notions, and of those things which are predicated of things, or of the subjects themselves, in what, or paronymously. This delimitation will be a certain division of beings, in this manner. Of the things that are, some are said of a subject but are not in a subject: as "man" is said of this man, and that synonymously; they are not in a subject, because they are not predicated paronymously of this man. Some, however, are in a subject but are not said of a subject: as the individual accidents and the singulars absolutely, such as the grammar in the mind of Donatus. These individual accidents are in a subject, but not as parts in a whole. For if they were as parts in a whole, they would be as parts of substances, which is absurd.

units.la: Quædam dicuntur de subiecto, & sunt in subiecto: vt scientia ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ [?]: nempe in animo: de subiecto etiam dicitur, nepe de grammatica, vt grammatica fit ὡς ὑποκείμενον: sed substantiæ ipsæ priore & nobiliore ratione dicuntur ὑποκείμενα. Quædam οὔτε ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ [?], ἔτι καθ' ὑποκειμένου λέγεται: vt iuxta substantiarum individua καθόλως dicta: vt hic homo, hic equus. Accidentia quidem individua possunt esse ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ, vti dictum est in secunda parte diuisionis τῶν ὄντων: sed inferiore modo dicuntur ὑποκείμενα, quum possint ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ nempe in substantiis individuis esse.
units.tr: Some things are both said of a subject and are in a subject: as knowledge is in a subject [?], namely in the mind; it is also said of a subject, namely of grammar, as grammar is a subject; but substances themselves are called subjects in the prior and nobler sense. Some things neither are in a subject nor are said of a subject: as the individuals of substances, universally stated, such as this man, this horse. Individual accidents can indeed be in a subject, as has been said in the second part of the division of beings; but they are called subjects in a lower sense, since they can be in a subject, namely in individual substances.

units.la: Distincta hoc modo τὰ ὄντα, ad distinctas categorias non ante reuocari possunt, quàm duæ regulæ in primis necessariæ præponantur, quibus τὰ συγγενῆ καὶ τὰ ἑτερογενῆ, ea quæ sunt eiusdem categoriæ, & quæ alterius, discernamus. Prior regula hæc est: Quando vnum de altero prædicatur συνωνύμως, vt de subiecto: quæcunque de illo prædicato dicētur, illa etiam de subiecto dicentur καθόλου & συνωνύμως vt homo de individuo aliquo homine, vt de Platone, prædicatur. Quare animal quod dicitur de homine συνωνύμως, de individuo illo homine prædicatur.
units.tr: Things distinguished in this way cannot be brought back to their distinct categories until two rules, which are necessary above all, have been set down first, by which we may tell apart those things that are of the same kind (τὰ συγγενῆ) and those that are of different kinds (τὰ ἑτερογενῆ), that is, what belongs to the same category and what to another. The first rule is this: when one thing is predicated of another synonymously, as of a subject, whatever is predicated of the former will also be predicated of the latter, universally and synonymously; thus, as man is predicated of some individual man, such as Plato. Therefore, animal, which is predicated synonymously of man, is predicated of that individual man.

units.la: Cæterum vt hanc regulam ad vsum suum reuocemus, δεῖ ἀπὸ τῶν καθέκαστα [?] μεταβαίνειν. καὶ ὁ συνωνυμία λανθάνουσι [?] μᾶλλον ἐν τοῖς καθόλου, ἢ ἐν τοῖς ἀδιαφόρεσι. Oportet ab ipsis singularibus ad vniuersalia transire. Nam si incipiamus ab ipsis καθόλου, incidemus in homonymias: & quae sunt ἑτερογενῆ, ἐς se συγγενῆ putabimus. Quare vitanda est Homonymia: constituenda est synonymia. Oportet vnum dici de altero ὡς καθ᾽ ὑποκειμένου. Tandem haec prior regula adhibenda est, vt series τῶν συγγενῶν, & illorum, quae praedicantur συνωνύμως, recte constituatur.
units.tr: Moreover, to put this rule to its proper use, we must proceed from the particulars (τὰ καθέκαστα) [to the universals]. Synonymy is more easily overlooked in universals than in indifferent things. We must pass from the singulars themselves to the universals. For if we begin from the universals themselves, we will fall into homonymies, and we will think that things which are of different kinds are of the same kind. Therefore homonymy must be avoided and synonymy must be established. One thing must be said of another as of a subject (ὡς καθ᾽ ὑποκειμένου). Finally, this first rule must be applied so that the series of things of the same kind, and of those which are predicated synonymously, may be correctly constituted.

units.la: Altera regula pertinet ad illa, quae non sunt eiusdem categoriae. regula haec est: Sub diuersis poste- generibus positorum, & non ὑπαλλήλων (id est, quorum vnum de altero non potest praedicari, vt genus de specie) illorum diuersae sunt εἰδοποιοὶ differentiae: vt animal & scientia non sunt eiusdem categoriae: quia diuersae sunt differentiae εἰδοποιοὶ animalis & scientiae. Animalis enim differentiae sunt pedatum, bipes, volans, aquatile: quarum differentiarum nulla scientiae convenire potest.
units.tr: The second rule concerns those things which are not of the same category. The rule is this: things placed under different highest genera, and not subordinate (that is, things of which one cannot be predicated of the other, as a genus of a species), have different specific differences (εἰδοποιοὶ differentiae). Thus animal and knowledge are not of the same category, because the specific differences of animal and of knowledge are different. For the differences of animal are footed, two-footed, flying, aquatic; and none of these differences can belong to knowledge.

units.la: Adhibitis his duabus regulis, vt nihil nō ad generaquaedā categoriarum reuocemus, necessario decem genera categoriarum sunt ponenda. Nam eorum, quae absque complexione dicuntur, vnumquodque aut substantiam, aut quantum, aut quale aut vbi, aut quando, aut positum, seu situm esse, aut habere, aut agere, aut pati significat. Est autem substantia (vt quodammodo adumbremus) cuius ratione reliqua omnia dicuntur accidere: vt homo, equus &c.
units.tr: By applying these two rules, so that we reduce nothing to some general categories, ten categories of genera must necessarily be posited. For each of those things that are said without combination signifies either substance, or quantity, or quality, or where, or when, or position, or being situated, or having, or acting, or being acted upon. Substance is (so that we may sketch it in some measure) that by reason of which all the other things are said to belong to it: such as man, horse, etc.

units.la: Quatitas est cuius causa substatia naturalis & corporea in partes dividua est: aut est numerus. Sic bicubitum & tricubitum, ad quantitatem referuntur. Tertia categoria est relationis, qua aliquid, id quod est, ratione alterius esse dicitur: ut duplum, dimidium. In hac categoria accidens non uno, sed duobus subiectis nititur, quorum uno fundari, altero terminari una relatio dicitur.
units.tr: Quantity is that by reason of which a natural and corporeal substance is divisible into parts, or it is number. Thus two cubits and three cubits are referred to quantity. The third category is that of relation, by which something, which is what it is, is said to be by reason of another, as double, half. In this category an accident rests not on one subject but on two, of which one is said to be the ground and the other the terminus of a single relation.

units.la: Reliqua sunt sex genera, quae absolutū quoddam genus significat, sed cum relatione quadam differentiae ad aliud. Ut cum quaedam substantia dicitur alicubi esse: ut, exempli gratia, in templo: sic definitur, ut sit alicubi, nempe in eo loco, in quo conciones sacrae habentur. Hic genus absolutum est: at in differentia fit mentio loci & locati. Item genus hoc ποτέ[?], non refertur ad aliud: sed differentia mensuratum aliquid tempore significat: ut mane, tempore quo sol oritur. Item κεῖσθαι[?] seu situm esse, de substantia dicitur cum differentia relationis partium ad totum ipsum: ut supinum esse, pronum esse, recumbere, sedere. Habere: ut armatum esse: significat enim rem absolutam quatenus habetur ab aliquo. Denique agere, ut secare, urere. Pati, ut secari, uri. Haec efferuntur absque compositione & divisione: neque verum quid, aut falsum significant. Quum vero componuntur inter se, constituitur affirmatio aut negatio. Omnis autem affirmatio vera aut falsa est propter compositionem.
units.tr: The remaining are six genera, which signify some absolute genus but with a certain relation of difference to another. For example, when some substance is said to be somewhere, as in a temple: it is so defined that it is somewhere, namely in that place in which sacred sermons are held. Here the genus is absolute, but in the difference mention is made of place and the thing placed. Likewise, this genus (when?) is not referred to another; but by the difference it signifies something measured by time, as in the morning, at the time when the sun rises. Likewise, κεῖσθαι (or being situated) is said of substance with a difference of the relation of its parts to the whole itself: as to be supine, to be prone, to recline, to sit. Having, as to be armed, for it signifies an absolute thing insofar as it is held by someone. Finally, acting, as to cut, to burn. Being acted upon, as to be cut, to be burned. These are expressed without combination and division, and they do not signify anything true or false. But when they are combined with one another, affirmation or negation is constituted. Every affirmation, moreover, is true or false on account of the combination.

units.la: CATEGORIA SVB-stantiæ.
units.tr: The Category of Substance.

units.la: Homonymum est vocabulum οὐσίας. Inter-dum illud quod neq; de aliquo dicitur, neque in aliquo est: interdum materiam & formam: nonnunquam ideam: interdum etiam definitionem significat. Dialecticus οὐσίας dividit primò in primas & secundas.
units.tr: The word οὐσία is homonymous. Sometimes it signifies that which is neither said of anything nor is in anything; sometimes matter and form; sometimes the idea; and sometimes also the definition. The dialectician divides οὐσία first into primary and secondary substances.

units.la: Quæ neque καθ' ὑποκειμένου λέγεται, ne-que ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ἔστιν, ipsa ὑποκείμενα di-cta, sunt primæ Substantiæ, hoc est, τὰ καθέκαστα καὶ ἄτομα ἀσω[?]. Ac substernuntur quidē non solum accuratis scientiarum prædicatis in quid verumetiam logicis & communibus, quan-dam κατηγορίας συγγένειαν habentibus.
units.tr: Those things which are neither said καθ' ὑποκειμένου nor are ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ, and which are called subjects themselves, are primary substances, that is, τὰ καθέκαστα καὶ ἄτομα. And these are indeed placed under not only the precise predicates of the sciences in respect of what a thing is, but also the logical and common ones, which have a certain kinship of category [κατηγορίας συγγένεια].

units.la: Quæ vero reliquis nouem categoriarum generibus substernuntur: quanu[?] καθέκαστα non tamen proprie dicitur ὑποκείμενα, sed vt τὸ δὲ ἐν τῷδέ τινι ἔχει[?]. Neque prima qualitas, neque prima quantitas proprie dicitur vt πρώτη οὐσία prima substātia: quia τὰ καθέκαστα etiam illo-rum accidentium sunt in prima substantia ὡς ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ.
units.tr: Those things, however, which are placed under the remaining nine genera of categories, are καθέκαστα, yet they are not properly called subjects, but are as τὸ δὲ ἐν τῷδέ τινι ἔχει. Neither the primary quality nor the primary quantity is properly called primary substance [πρώτη οὐσία], because the καθέκαστα of those accidents also are in primary substance as in a subject.

units.la: Ipsa quoque per se prima substantia dicitur ἐν ἀριθμῷ[?]: & quia de nullo prædicatur, nec est in aliquo subiecto, ipsa per se esse non propter aliud, neque propter accidens esse dicitur.
units.tr: The primary substance itself is also called, per se, ἐν ἀριθμῷ; and because it is predicated of nothing, nor is it in any subject, it is said to be per se and not on account of another, nor on account of an accident.

units.la: Secundæ verò substantiæ sunt γένη[?] primarum substantiarum, quæ de primis illis dicuntur {ὁμωνύμως}. Sunt enim ex illis quæ dicuntur de subiecto: de quibus in diuisione [?]τῶν ὄντων dicum est. Multa verò prædicatur de primis sub-stantiis in quid [?]λογικῶς seu dialecticῶς ratione [?]κατηγορίας, quæ tamen, si accuratè expendas, non sunt genera. Deus dicitur substantia: cuius tamen substantia est [?]ὑπερέχοντος. Dicitur etiā Spi-ritus, qui tamen à spiritibus creatis plus quàm genere differt.
units.tr: Secondary substances, however, are the genera of the primary substances, which are said of those primary ones {ὁμωνύμως}. For they are among those things which are said of a subject, concerning which it was said in the division of beings. Many things, however, are predicated of primary substances logically or dialectically in respect of what they are, by reason of the category; yet these, if you weigh them carefully, are not genera. God is called a substance, whose substance, however, is ὑπερέχοντος [of surpassing]. He is also called Spirit, who nevertheless differs from created spirits by more than genus.

units.la: [?]Συνωνυμία prædicationis constituetur siâ primis substantiis, [?]ἄτομα εἴδη acuratè expen-dātur: vt enim [?]καθέκαστα sunt mensura [?]ἄτο-[?]μων εἰδῶν ita etiam [?]ἄτομα εἴδη sunt mensura ge-nerum. Per se esse, & in aliquo non esse dicitur substantia: at ratio non erit [?]συνωνυμος in æter-nis & caducis substantiis: quia prius de æternis, vt de Deo, mentibus, quàm de caducis, quæ non essent, nisi essent æterna quædam, dicitur.
units.tr: The synonymy of predication is established by the primary substances, if the ἄτομα εἴδη are carefully weighed: for just as the καθέκαστα are the measure of the ἄτομα species, so also the ἄτομα εἴδη are the measure of the genera. Substance is said to be per se and not to be in anything; but the account will not be συνωνυμος in eternal and perishable substances, because it is said first of eternal things, such as God and minds, and then of perishable things, which would not exist unless certain eternal things existed.

units.la: De materia quoque ac forma prius dicitur, quàm de compositis ex materia & forma primis substantiis physicis. Quo fit vt ex secundis substantiis, [?]ἄτομα εἴδη, magis substantiæ dicantur, quàm genera: quia perfectiorē & certiorem notitiam afferunt quàm genera. Ideo verò dicuntur substantiæ, non quòd ipsæ sint extra metem substantiæ, & [?]ὑποκείμενά τινα, sed quòd in quid [?]συνωνύμως non [?]παρωνύμως de primis substantiis, vt de subiectis prædicentur: ac de his reliqua omnia.
units.tr: Of matter and form also, it is said first, before it is said of the composites of matter and form, the primary physical substances. Hence it comes about that from the secondary substances, the ἄτομα εἴδη, things are called substances more than genera are: because they bring a more perfect and certain knowledge than genera do. They are called substances, however, not because they are themselves outside the notion of substance, and certain ὑποκείμενά, but because they are predicated of the primary substances, as of subjects, in quid and συνωνύμως, not παρωνύμως; and all the rest are predicated of these.

units.la: Prima proprietas huius categoriæ hæc est: substansubstantiam in nullo inesse: sed omnia in substan- tia inesse, eíque inhærere. Prima certè substan-tia, quia est ὑποκείμενον & τὸ δέ τι οὐ[?], nulli inesse potest.
units.tr: The first property of this category is this: substance is in nothing, but all things are in substance and inhere in it. The primary substance, certainly, because it is ὑποκείμενον and τὸ δέ τι οὐ, cannot be in anything.

units.la: Secundæ vero substantiæ dicuntur de subiecto, & prædicantur in quid: vt homo de homine aliquo: & de homine animal, neq; animal in homine (cùm homo sit ὅπερ ζῷον) aut hominem in aliquo homine inesse tectè dixerimus. Neque solùm nomina secundarum substantiarū dicuntur de primo subiecto: verumetiā definitiones.
units.tr: The secondary substances, however, are said of a subject and are predicated in respect of what a thing is, as man is predicated of a certain man; and we shall not rightly say that animal is in man (since man is ὅπερ ζῷον), or that man is in some man. Nor are only the names of the secondary substances said of the primary subject, but also the definitions.

units.la: Cætera quæ prædicantur de substantiis, συ-παρ-ωνύμως[?] prædicatur: vt albedo inest quidem in substantia: ideò que aliquid album dici potest paronymως[?]: at definitio & ratio albedinis non potest de prima substantia dici, vt de subiecto. Neque solum genus & species subiecto nō inesse dicuntur: verumetiam differētiæ. Generis quidem sunt qualitates quædam: verum quia earum nomē & ratio essentiæ de subiecto prædicatur: subiecto primo non inesse dicuntur. Ex quo intelligitur illos errare qui negant differentiam prædicari in quid. Quanuis aūt partes substantiarū videantur esse in toto: vt pes, caput, manus in corpore animalis, nec prædicentur de toto συνωνυμως· tamen non sunt accidentia substantiarum.
units.tr: Other things which are predicated of substances are predicated συμπαρωνύμως: as whiteness indeed is in a substance, and therefore something can be called white paronymως; but the definition and account of whiteness cannot be said of the primary substance as of a subject. Nor are genus and species said not to be in a subject only; differences also are. Qualities indeed are of the genus; but because their name and account of essence are predicated of a subject, they are said not to be in the primary subject. From this it is understood that those err who deny that difference is predicated in respect of what a thing is. However, although the parts of substances seem to be in the whole, as foot, head, hand in the body of an animal, and are not predicated of the whole συνωνυμως, nevertheless they are not accidents of substances.

units.la: Alia enim ratione accidentia, atque partes substantiarum in subiecto dicūtur esse. Partes enim substantiarum, quæ & ipsæ substantiæ sunt, non insunt in subiecto ἁπλῶς, ea ratione qua est subiectum, sed qua subiectum est totum quiddam, quod causa quantitatis ex partibus integrū quid constituentibus, constat. Accidentia vero infunt in subiecto, nō alia ratione, quàm qua est subiectum ἁπλῶς τ᾽ ὅτι, & οὐσία.
units.tr: For by another reason accidents and the parts of substances are said to be in a subject. For the parts of substances, which are themselves substances, are not in the subject ἁπλῶς, by the reason by which the subject is a subject, but by the reason by which the subject is a certain whole thing, which, by reason of quantity, consists of parts constituting a complete thing. Accidents, however, are in a subject for no other reason than that by which the subject is ἁπλῶς τ᾽ ὅτι and οὐσία.

units.la: Quare non solum partes illas, quæ ratione ὑλῆς & οὐσίας sunt priores (ut sunt materia & forma) subsistentias esse dicemus, verumetiam τῆς σωματικῆς οὐσίας, totius integralis partes, quæ subsistentia ex materia & forma cōposita sunt posteriores. Ex quibus intelligitur, secundas substantias nullo modo inesse subiecto primo, sed praedicari συνωνύμως tantum: ac species quidem ἀτόμους de primis substantiis, genera autem & differentiae de speciebus, & propter species per regulam κατηγορίας de primis substantiis praedicari συνωνύμως, quod si συνωνύμως, nō solum nomē, sed etiam definitionem praedicari necesse est. Id enim est συνωνύμον, ut supra diximus.
units.tr: Wherefore we shall say that not only those parts which, in the sense of ὕλη and οὐσία, are prior (as matter and form are) are subsistences, but also the parts of τῆς σωματικῆς οὐσίας, the parts of an integral whole, which, being composed of matter and form, are posterior and subsist. From these things it is understood that secondary substances are in no way in the primary subject, but are predicated only συνωνύμως: and species, indeed, ἀτόμους, are predicated of the primary substances, but genera and differences of the species, and, on account of the species, by the rule of the category, are predicated of the primary substances συνωνύμως; and if they are predicated συνωνύμως, not only the name but also the definition must be predicated. For that is συνώνυμον, as we said above.

units.la: Alia proprietas substantiae est: quod omnis substantia videatur significare τόδε τι comparata cum accidentibus. Accidentia enim significat τόδε ἐν τῷ δε. Ac primas quidem substantias in primis significare τόδε τι nō est dubium. At secundae substantiae non videntur significare τόδε τι, quia sunt qualitates quædam, quibus mens seu intellectus substantias noscit: & quum sint qualitates intellectus, sunt accidentia. Verum magnum discrimen est inter hæc accidentia, & illa quæ dicuntur ἁπλῶς accidentia. Nam secundae substantiae ὅπερ ὄν, seu τί ἐστι significant, eo quod de primis substantiis prædicentur, & τῷ ἀφορίζειν.i. eo quod primas substantias se-parent ab accidentibus, quæ inhærent & insunt. Accidentia vero ὁ ἀπλῶς[?] dicta, significant illud quod separatur in notione primarum substantiarum.
units.tr: Another property of substance is that every substance seems to signify τόδε τι, compared with accidents. For accidents signify τόδε ἐν τῷ δε. That the primary substances, first of all, signify τόδε τι is not in doubt. But secondary substances do not seem to signify τόδε τι, because they are certain qualities by which the mind or intellect knows substances; and since they are qualities of the intellect, they are accidents. Yet there is a great difference between these accidents and those which are called accidents ἁπλῶς. For secondary substances signify ὅπερ ὄν, or τί ἐστι, in that they are predicated of primary substances, and τῷ ἀφορίζειν, that is, in that they separate the primary substances from the accidents which inhere and are in them. The accidents, however, called ὁ ἀπλῶς, signify that which is separated in the notion of the primary substances.

units.la: Quare secundæ substantiæ non significant ποιόν τι ἁπλῶς, habita ratione ὑποκειμένου, & accidentium: sed ratione intellectus noticeris[?]. & οὐσίαν ab accidentibus, per καθόλου quædam νοήματα (quæ sunt genus & species) separantis. Quo fit etiam ut genus qualitatem quādam ποιότητα significet, quæ latius pateat, quàm illa quam species ἄτομος significat.
units.tr: Wherefore secondary substances do not signify ποιόν τι ἁπλῶς, with regard to the subject and the accidents, but, with regard to the intellect, they separate the substance from the accidents through certain universal notions (which are genus and species). Hence it also comes about that the genus signifies a certain quality, ποιότητα, which extends more widely than that which the species ἄτομος signifies.

units.la: Est etiam ἀχώριστον quidem, id est, inseparabile: sed non proprium substantiae solius, ut substantiae inter se non sint contrariae. Sunt contraria hic intelligenda illa, quæ sub uno eodemque genere posita, & longissimo intervallo dissita, mutuò sese ex uno eodemque subiecto expellunt.
units.tr: There is also ἀχώριστον, that is, inseparable; but this is not peculiar to substance alone, since substances are not contrary to one another. Those things are to be understood here as contraries which, placed under one and the same genus and set at the greatest distance, mutually expel one another from one and the same subject.

units.la: Cùm igitur contraria sint in subiecto, erunt accidentia: subiectum verò ipsum erit substantia: quæ non dicetur contraria alteri substantiae, siquidem non inest in subiecto: quum sit ipsa subiectū contrariorum. Quod verò ignis & aqua contraria dicuntur, non ideo dicuntur, quòd contraria sint corpora hæc, sed quod ποιητικά, efficientia sint contrariarum qualitatum: aut etiam παθητικά. Quare dicuntur contraria propter qualitates contrarias, quarum causa vel mixtio corporibus patibilibus, vel motus, vel quies, quæ sunt contraria,accidere solent.
units.tr: Since, therefore, contraries are in a subject, they will be accidents; but the subject itself will be substance, which will not be said to be contrary to another substance, since it is not in a subject, inasmuch as it is itself the subject of contraries. But that fire and water are called contrary is not because these bodies are contrary, but because they are ποιητικά, efficient of contrary qualities, or even παθητικά. Wherefore they are called contrary on account of contrary qualities, to the causing of which, either a mixture in patient bodies, or motion, or rest, which are contrary, are wont to occur.

units.la: Diuersa quidem sunt non solùm numero,sed etiam specie [?] illa contraria,quæ insunt in subiecto:at subiectum unum numero & idem est. Subiecto autem primùm logicis & Dialecticis est τόδε τι[?], quod per se subsistit. Physicis autem est materia prima, quæ sola & seipsa non subsistit. ac in materia prima tanquam in subiecto contraria dicuntur Physicis priuatio & forma, quæ tamen στερητικῶς[?] sunt opposita. nam si logicè essent contraria, necessariò essent species sub uno eodemque genere. At priuatio non potest esse species.
units.tr: Those contraries which are in a subject are different not only in number but also in species [?]; but the subject is one and the same in number. Now the subject, for logicians and dialecticians, is τόδε τι, which subsists per se. For physicists, however, it is prime matter, which alone and of itself does not subsist. And in prime matter, as in a subject, the contraries are said by physicists to be privation and form, which are nevertheless opposed στερητικῶς. For if they were logically contraries, they would necessarily be species under one and the same genus. But privation cannot be a species.

units.la: Cæterum non est hoc ἴδιον, sed est ἀχώριστον[?] duntaxat substantiæ. Nam non solùm substantia, sed quantitas quoque est contrariorum expers. Bicubitum enim non est contrarium tricubito: neque numerus numero, neque figura figuræ. Cùm enim contraria sint extremis definita (vt ex eorum definitione intelligitur) & extrema genere vel subiecto eodem determinentur: quorum nulla erunt extrema, illa genere vel subiecto eodem determinari non poterunt: atqui infiniti nullum est extremum. Quantitates aut infinitè augeri vel minui possunt: quare quantitati nihil est contrarium.
units.tr: Moreover, this is not a property (ἴδιον) but merely something inseparable (ἀχώριστον) from substance. For not only substance but also quantity is free of contraries. A two-cubit length is not the contrary of a three-cubit length; nor is one number the contrary of another, nor one figure of another. For since contraries are defined by their extremes (as is understood from their definition), and extremes are determined by a common genus or subject, then where there are no extremes, those things cannot be determined by a common genus or subject; but of the infinite there is no extreme. Quantities can be increased or diminished infinitely; therefore quantity has nothing contrary to it.

units.la: Tertium hoc substantiæ etiam attribuitur, substantiam nec magis nec minus dici substantiam: neque intentionem aut remissionem admittere. Quamuis enim substantia, contrariis accidentibus & motionibus subiiciatur, tamen for[?] mæ causa,tota & perfecta est. Entelechia enim substantiae simplex est, cui nihil addi, nihil detrahi potest. Quod aut substantia magis & minus suscipere videtur, & perfectionis ac imperfectionis particeps est, id fit materiae & accidetium causa. Sed neque ipsa per se accidentia, quibus ceu finibus & extremis motiones determinatur, magis ac minus suscipiut. Habitus enim hic non est magis habitus, quàm ille: neque haec figura magis est figura, quàm illa. Quare adultus vir nno est magis homo seipso puero. Nam quod puer ἐνεργείας hominis minùs praestat quàm vir: id facultatibus cum materia & accidentibus concretis tribuendū est, non autem ipsi substantiae.
units.tr: This third feature is also attributed to substance: that substance is not called more or less substance, and does not admit intension or remission. For although substance is subject to contrary accidents and motions, nevertheless, by its form, it is whole and perfect. For the entelechy of substance is simple: nothing can be added to it, nothing taken away. That substance seems to receive more and less, and to partake of perfection and imperfection, happens on account of matter and accidents. But the accidents themselves, by which motions are bounded as by ends and extremes, do not receive more and less either. For this habit is not more a habit than that one, nor is this shape more a shape than that one. Hence an adult man is not more a man than he was as a boy. For that a boy performs the activities of a man less than a grown man does must be attributed to his faculties, together with matter and concrete accidents, and not to substance itself.

units.la: Neque eo quod iustior sit aliquis quàm ante fuerit, habitum magis habitum esse dicemus. Quod enim iustior est, non ratione habitus, sed causa facultatum δυνάμεως animae id accidit.
units.tr: Nor shall we say that a habit is more a habit because someone is more just than before. For that he is more just happens not by reason of the habit, but by the cause of the faculties of the soul (δύναμις).

units.la: Quod dicimus substantiam unam nō esse magis substantiam, quàm alteram, intelligendū est de substantiis eiusdē ordinis: ut de primis inter se, & secundis inter se. Nā si prima cum secunda substantia comparatur, prima magis erit substantia, quàm secunda.
units.tr: When we say that one substance is no more a substance than another, this must be understood of substances of the same order, such as the primary among themselves and the secondary among themselves. For if a primary substance is compared with a secondary substance, the primary will be more a substance than the secondary.

units.la: Quartum hoc in primis substantiarū est pro-prium: Substantiam unam numero contraria posse suscipere: idque propter materiam, cū qua formae rerum naturalium οὐσιώδης[?] concretae sunt.
units.tr: This fourth is the proper feature of substances in particular: that one substance, numerically one, can receive contraries; and this on account of the matter with which the essential forms of natural things are joined.

units.la: Accidentia verò, quia neque sunt ipsa natura, substan neque res seu substantiae naturales, & quia ipsa substantia per se materiam non habent, non possunt esse. [?]ἐνυποκειμένον[?] τι, nec dicūtur posse suscipere contraria. De accidētibus hæc Aristoteles: [?]ὅσα δ' ἡ φύσει μὲν, μὴ οὐσία δέ, ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ἐστὶ τούτοις ὕλη.[?] Quæcunque sunt quidem natura, neque tamen sunt substantia, illa non habēt materiam. Quare præter οὐσίαν nihil idem numero δεκτικὸν contrariorum posse esse. Quod si quis obiiciat, oratio-nem & opinionem, quæ non sunt οὐσίαι, posse suscipere contraria eò, quòd vera & interdum sal-sa oratio, vt & opinio, esse possit: respondemus id non propter ipsam orationē, aut opinionem, sed propter rem illam ad quam refertur, quæ est extra mentem, accidere: nempe propter ῥητὸν & δοξαστόν, quæ sunt res extra mentem mutationibus obnoxiæ, propter quas oratio vel opinio ex vera in falsam mutata dicitur.
units.tr: But accidents, because they are neither themselves nature, substance, nor natural things or substances, and because they do not have matter of their own through themselves, cannot be something underlying (ἐνυποκείμενον), nor are they said to be able to receive contraries. Aristotle says this about accidents: "Whatever things are by nature, but are not substance, are in a subject; for these have matter." Whatever things are natural, but are not substance, do not have matter. Therefore, besides substance, nothing numerically one can be capable of contraries. But if someone objects that speech and opinion, which are not substances, can receive contraries because a speech or opinion can be true and sometimes false, we reply that this happens not because of speech or opinion itself, but because of that thing to which it refers, which lies outside the mind: namely, because of the sayable (ῥητόν) and the opinable (δοξαστόν), which are things outside the mind subject to change, and on account of which a speech or opinion is said to be changed from true to false.

units.la: CATEGORIA QVAN-titatis.
units.tr: THE CATEGORY OF QUANTITY.

units.la: Categoria Quantitatis est ὁμώνυμος, ac de numero prius dicitur, de reliquis vero propter numerum. Videtur quidē esse συνώνυμος cùm dicitur de continua & discreta, quæ tamen non est: quia quantum infinitè diuiduum, nō habet idem genus συνώνυμον cum quanto finitè diuiduo. Rebus autem corporeis proprie tribuitur quantitas, quatenus habent partes extra partes: incorporeis verè non tribuitur, quia incorporeum non est diuiduum partibus, sed quidquid est, totum est, nec habet partem extra partem. Exemplum substantiæ partibus diuiduæ, esto corpus hominis: incorporeæ verò substantiæ anima, quæ tota est in corpore toto & in qualibet parte eius. Item vniuersum hoc aspectabile dicitur, & est partibus diuiduum, & habet partes extra partes. At Deus quia est incorporeus, non est partibus diuiduus, sed vbique totus. Adhæc quidditates, quatenus mente concipiuntur, sunt totum quiddam, nō tamen partibus diuiduum, sed ὅλως ὅλον[?] ideóq; sunt similes numeris, quibus nihil addi, nihil adimi potest. Nam si adderetur aut adimeretur, non esset idem numerus. Omnis igitur quantitas partes habet, & consideratur in corporeis substantiis, quæ habent partes extra partes.
units.tr: The category of quantity is equivocal (ὁμώνυμος), and is said first of number, and of the rest on account of number. It seems indeed to be univocal (συνώνυμος) when it is predicated of the continuous and the discrete, but it is not: because a quantity infinitely divisible does not have the same univocal genus as a quantity finitely divisible. Quantity is properly attributed to corporeal things, insofar as they have parts outside parts; it is truly not attributed to incorporeal things, because the incorporeal is not divisible into parts, but whatever it is, it is whole, and it does not have part outside part. An example of a substance divisible into parts is the body of a man; an example of an incorporeal substance is the soul, which is wholly in the whole body and in each of its parts. Likewise this whole visible world is said to be divisible, and it has parts outside parts. But God, because he is incorporeal, is not divisible into parts, but is wholly everywhere. Moreover, quiddities, insofar as they are conceived by the mind, are a whole something, yet not divisible into parts, but wholly whole (ὅλως ὅλον); and therefore they are like numbers, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be taken away. For if something were added or taken away, it would not be the same number. Therefore every quantity has parts, and it is considered in corporeal substances, which have parts outside parts.

units.la: Dialecticus diuidit quantitate in continuam & discretam. Quantitas continua est, cuius partes termino communi indiuiduo per se possunt vnum & totum fieri: vt partes lineæ possunt vnum quid fieri ratione puncti: & partes superficiei, ratione lineæ: & corporis partes ratione superficiei possunt vnum quid & totum fieri. In continuis etiā numerantur tempus & locus. Nā tempus præsens videtur esse ὁ νῦν χρόνος[?], qui præteritum & futurum connectit. Et loci partes habent κοινὸν ὅρον[?]: siquidem corporis partes, quæ sunt in loco, κοινὸν ὅρον[?] habent.
units.tr: The dialectician divides quantity into continuous and discrete. A continuous quantity is one whose parts, by a common terminus, can by themselves become one and a whole without division: thus the parts of a line can become one thing by reason of a point, and the parts of a surface by reason of a line, and the parts of a body by reason of a surface can become one thing and a whole. Time and place are also numbered among continuous quantities. For the present time seems to be the "now" (ὁ νῦν χρόνος), which connects the past and the future. And the parts of place have a common boundary (κοινὸν ὅρον), since the parts of a body which are in a place have a common boundary.

units.la: Quantitas discreta est cuius partes termini communis interuentu coniungi non sic possunt, vt finis partis principium fit alterius: vt denarii numeri partes sunt duo quinarii: qui duo numeri sunt ita discreti, vt nullo termino communi con iungi possint, quo couftituatur vnum cōtinuum. Quare partes discretæ quantitatis conflituunt vnum indiuiduis partibus discretum. Eiusmodi est quantitas discreta: quæ nihil aliud est, quàm numerus. Discretæ etiam quātitati hoc proprie inest, vt diuidendo eam ad minimum, nempe ad vnitatem perueniatur, quæ quidē vnitas est indi uiduum quiddam. At quantitati continuæ hoc proprium inest, vt quantum continuum causa partium, fit infinite diuiduum, quia non eflet quantum continuū, fi poflet dari minimum quid & indiuiduum.
units.tr: A discrete quantity is one whose parts cannot be joined by means of a common terminus, so that the end of one part becomes the beginning of another: thus the parts of the number ten are two fives; these two numbers are so discrete that they cannot be joined by any common terminus to constitute one continuum. Therefore the parts of a discrete quantity constitute one thing discrete by indivisible parts. Such is discrete quantity, which is nothing other than number. It is also proper to discrete quantity that by dividing it we arrive at a minimum, namely the unit, which is indeed an indivisible thing. But it is proper to continuous quantity that a continuous quantity, on account of its parts, is infinitely divisible, because it would not be a continuous quantity if some minimum and indivisible thing could be given.

units.la: Cæterùm ex quantis, quædã constant ex partibus Θέσιν quandam habentibus: quædam verò ex partibus non habentibus Θέσιν. Partes lineæ habent Θέσιν. Nam vnaquæque pars lineæ posita est in aliquo loco: sic partes corporis. At numerus non habet Θέσιν partium: neque partes temporis habent Θέσιν inter fe: nam non manent in aliquo loco simul omnes temporis partes. At τάξιν quādam habent, quia tempus prius dicitur posteriore: sic etiam vnum prius numeratur, quàm duo: & duo, quàm tria: sic orationis partes, quatenus oratio pronunciatur, non habent Θέσιν, sed τάξιν quandam. Vt enim partes habeant Θέσιν, necesse est remanere in loco.
units.tr: Moreover, among quantities, some consist of parts having position (Θέσιν), and others of parts not having position. The parts of a line have position; for each part of a line is placed in some place, and so are the parts of a body. But number does not have position in its parts, nor do the parts of time have position among themselves; for not all the parts of time remain in some place at once. But they have a certain order (τάξιν), because time is said to be prior to later time; so also one is numbered before two, and two before three; so too the parts of speech, insofar as speech is uttered, do not have position, but a certain order. For parts to have position, they must remain in a place.

units.la: Præterea fciedum est numerum hic intelligi mathemathematicum à sensilibus formis secretum: qui quidem numerus deinde applicatur sensilibus formis in copositis mathematicis, vt in Mu-sica, Geometria, Astronomia, Optica & similibus. Ac numeri in eiusmodi sensilibus confide-rati dicuntur numeri numerati, quibus quaedam accidunt, quae ipsis per se numeris secretis non accidunt. Sic oratio reuocatur quidem ad nume-rum, quia partes orationis quae profertur, nume-rantur secundum prius & posterius, distinctis nu-mero syllabis non continuatis. Alia ratione ora-tio, qua nimirum sonus est, ad praedicamentum qualitatis refertur. Haec igitur & similia ad quanti-tatem discretam referuntur, quatenus in parti-bus discretum aliquid habent.
units.tr: Furthermore, it should be known that number here is understood as mathematical number, separated from sensible forms; and this number is then applied to sensible forms in mathematical composites, as in music, geometry, astronomy, optics, and similar disciplines. And numbers considered in such sensible things are called numbered numbers (numeri numerati), to which some attributes belong that do not belong to separated numbers in themselves. Thus speech is indeed reduced to number, because the parts of the speech that is uttered are counted according to before and after, with the syllables distinguished by number, not continuous. In another way, speech, insofar as it is sound, is referred to the category of quality. These and similar things, therefore, are referred to discrete quantity, insofar as they have something discrete in their parts.

units.la: Ad quantitatem continuam referuntur mo-tus, tempus, & locus. Motus quidem quatenus intelligitur fluxus quidam & trafitio: ratione cuius, forma quae fit, dicitur habere partē post partem, prioribus partibus euanescentibus, & postē posterioribus exorientibus. Sed quando motus consideratur vt ἐνέργεια quaedam ἀτελής, est in categoria passionis: quia subiectu naturale, eius cau-sa, pati aliquid dicitur. Sic tempus, quatenus partes priores & posteriores habent cōmunem ter-minum praesens tempus, ad quātum continuum refertur: sed quatenus consideratur vt mensura communis & numerus distinguēs partes coelestis motionis, ad categoriam relatorum refertur. Sic etiā locus vna quidem ratione, qua partes eius communi termino connectuntur ad quantitatem cōtinuam refertur: altera vero, quæ ad locatum refertur, in categoria relatorum esse dicitur. Denique ad hanc categoriam quanti-tatis, reuocari possunt vocabula illa omnia, quæ concretam quantitatem significant: vt iter quatenus διάστημα, interuallum, iugerum & cætera huiusmodi.
units.tr: Motion, time, and place are referred to continuous quantity. Motion, insofar as it is understood as a certain flowing and passage, by reason of which the form that comes to be is said to have part after part, the prior parts vanishing and the later parts arising, is referred to continuous quantity. But when motion is considered as a certain incomplete activity (ἐνέργεια ἀτελής), it is in the category of passion, because the natural subject, by its cause, is said to undergo something. Likewise time, insofar as its prior and later parts have the present time as a common terminus, is referred to continuous quantity; but insofar as it is considered as a common measure and a number distinguishing the parts of heavenly motion, it is referred to the category of relatives. Likewise place, in one respect, insofar as its parts are connected by a common terminus, is referred to continuous quantity; in another respect, insofar as it is referred to the located thing, it is said to be in the category of relatives. Finally, to this category of quantity may be referred all those words which signify concrete quantity, such as a journey insofar as it is a distance (διάστημα), an interval, a furlong, and others of this kind.

units.la: Sunt etiam quædam quanta per accidens: vt cum magna febris dicitur, quia duratio multū extenditur. Neque enim febris per se quanta dicitur, sed propter tempus diuturnū. Quare quæ per se conueniunt quantis per se, coueniunt per accidens quantis per accidens: vt multū, parum, magnum, paruum, sunt relata quæ proprie insunt quantis per se: quæ quantis per accidens conuenire dicuntur per accidens.
units.tr: There are also some quantities that are quantities only accidentally, as when a high fever is called great because its duration is greatly extended. For a fever is not called a quantity in itself, but on account of the long duration. Therefore, those things which belong to quantities in themselves belong accidentally to quantities that are accidental: thus much, little, great and small are relatives which properly inhere in quantities in themselves, and which are said to belong accidentally to accidental quantities.

units.la: Vt substantiæ, ita quoque quātitatis ἀχώρι-στον quod est, sed non ἴδιον, nihil habere contrarium.
units.tr: Like substance, quantity too, which is inseparable but not proper to it, has no contrary.

units.la: Nam in contrariis oportet esse interuallum fini-tum, quo distent contraria: at in quantitatibus nullum interuallum finitū datur: quare in quan-titatibus non erunt contraria. Quod si quis ma-gnum & paruū (quæ quanto tribuuntur) aut multum & parum, contraria esse dicat: responden-dum est, esse quidem contraria relata quantitatum, sed non esse quantitates per se contrarias. Magnum igitur & paruum, multum & parū non sunt absolutè contraria, sed cōtraria relata, quæ quantitati, quia quantitas accidunt. Quod si absoluta quanta essent, contingeret rem eandem simul contrariorum participem esse. Sunt enim quædam quanta, quæ comparata cum aliis sunt magna, cum aliis parua. Neq; locus loco est contrarius, eò quod superum atque inferum cōtra-ria esse dicantur: vt locus Solis non est contrarius loco Lunæ. Quod enim superum atq; inferum, contraria dicantur, non eo quòd locus loco sit contrarius, sed quia contenta corpora, nempe leuia & grauia contrariis motibus mouentur, contraria illa dicuntur: h.e. nō quia sunt superficies seu locus: sed propter corpora leuia & grauia, quæ continentur: superna & inferna contraria dicuntur.
units.tr: For in contraries there must be a finite interval by which the contraries are apart, but in quantities no finite interval is given; therefore there will be no contraries in quantities. But if anyone says that great and small (which are attributed to quantity) or much and little are contraries, the answer must be that the relatives of quantities are indeed contraries, but quantities in themselves are not contraries. Great and small, much and little, therefore, are not absolutely contraries, but contrary relatives, which belong to quantity because quantity is their subject. For if they were absolute quantities, it would follow that the same thing would at the same time participate in contraries. For some quantities are great when compared with some things and small when compared with others. Nor is place contrary to place, even though up and down are said to be contraries: thus the place of the Sun is not contrary to the place of the Moon. For up and down are called contraries not because one place is contrary to another, but because the bodies contained, namely light and heavy bodies, are moved by contrary motions; so they are called contraries, that is, not because they are surfaces or place, but on account of the light and heavy bodies which are contained: the upper and the lower are called contraries.

units.la: Præterea quantitas non suscipit magis & mi-nus: vt bicubitum vnum altero bicubito nō ma-gis dicitur bicubitum: nec ternarius altero ter-nario dicitur magis ternarius: nec triangulus tri-angulo dicitur magis triangulus, aut circulus circulo. Sed hoc intelligendum de quantitatibus quæ sunt specie eædem: nam causa generis magis & minus quiddam dicuntur: vt numerum diximus prius dici quantitatem, quàm cætera quæ dicuntur posteriore ratione quantitates.
units.tr: Moreover, quantity does not admit of more and less: thus one two-cubit length is not said to be more two-cubit than another two-cubit length, nor is one ternary more ternary than another ternary, nor is one triangle said to be more triangular than another triangle, or one circle more circular than another circle. But this must be understood of quantities that are the same in species; for on account of their genus things are said to be more or less something: as we said before that number is called a quantity before the other things which are called quantities by a later reckoning.

units.la: Postremò proprium ἀχώρισον quantitatis est, vt secundum quantitatem æquale & inæqua-le quantum dicatur. Est enim æqualitas, vnitas quædam, quæ accidit multis numero differentibus, propter materiam mathematicam: vt, si differentes numero lineæ æquales dicantur, aut inæquales. Est alia vnitas similitudinis, de qua in categoria qualitatis dicetur.
units.tr: Lastly, the proper inseparable accident of quantity is that, according to quantity, something is said to be equal and unequal in quantity. For equality is a certain unity which belongs to many things differing in number, on account of mathematical matter: as when lines differing in number are called equal or unequal. There is another unity of similarity, which will be discussed in the category of quality.

units.la: CATEGORIA RE-lationis.
units.tr: CATEGORIA RELATIONIS.

units.la: PErmagni vsus est categoria τῶν πρός τι[?] in scientiis & disciplinis omnibus. Neque relatio-nes sunt figmenta, vt voluerunt quidam. In Dei-tate sunt relata tria, quæ non sunt accidentia, sed veræ ὑπόστασεις[?], quibus creatio rerum omnium & gubernatio tribuitur. In Mathematicis analo-gia, cōparatio, æqualitatis & inæqualitatis con-sideratio, nusquam non habet locum. In iurispru dentia, iustū ipsum proportione & relatione in-telligitur. Verùm quidem est καθ' ἕκαστα[?] relationum communi potius & interno sensu, quàm externis percipi: sed non eo minus ipsa esse exi-stimare debemus, quòd sensibus externis non percipiantur, cùm sensus internus potiori modo, quàm externus καθ' ἕκαστα[?] percipiat.
units.tr: The category of relation (ta pros ti) is of very great use in all sciences and disciplines. Nor are relations mere fictions, as some have held. In the Deity there are three related persons, which are not accidents but true hypostases, to whom the creation of all things and their governance are attributed. In mathematics, analogy, comparison, and the consideration of equality and inequality have their place everywhere. In jurisprudence, the just itself is understood by proportion and relation. It is true that relations are perceived particularly by the common and internal sense rather than by the external senses; yet we ought not on that account to think that they do not exist, because they are not perceived by the external senses, since the internal sense perceives particulars in a more excellent way than the external.

units.la: Cæterùm relatio omnis est inter duo absoluta, quorum vnum fundamētum, quo fundatur & incipit relatio, alterum terminus in quem definit relatio, dicitur. Relatio tamen vnum quiddam est, & definitur vt vnum: neque relatio ipsa refertur (quia esset relationis relatio) sed est εἶδός[?] quoddam seu species vna duorum relatorum. Rursus non quoduis vnum ex duobus absolutis constitutum, est relatio: non enim quod ex materia & forma, aut ex subiecto aut accidente, aut ex genere & differentia constituitur, est vnum ut relatio (quod enim hoc modo cōstituitur, est absolutū quid & ὑποκειμένου[?]) sed quod in duo-bus absolutis ὑποστάσει[?] unius ad alterū relata, propter accidēs quoddam intelligitur, id unum, nēpe una relata ratio dicitur. Est igitur relatio una quaedam comparationis ratio duorū absolutorum, aut reipsa, aut ἐννοίᾳ[?], seu ratione secretorum. Atq; haec una ratio nihil aliud est, quàm unum ὑφισάμενον[?] accidens compositū ex duo-bus accidentibus, quae rebus duabus absolutis & secretis accidunt.
units.tr: Moreover, every relation is between two absolutes, of which one is called the foundation, by which the relation is grounded and begins, and the other the term, at which the relation ends. Yet the relation is a certain one thing, and is defined as one: the relation itself is not itself related (for that would be a relation of a relation), but it is a certain form or single species of the two related things. Again, not just any one thing composed of two absolutes is a relation: for what is constituted from matter and form, or from subject and accident, or from genus and difference, is not one as a relation is (for what is constituted in this way is something absolute and a subject). Rather, that which is understood as one by some accident, in two absolutes related to one another by their underlying existence, is called one, namely one related ratio. Relation is therefore a certain single ratio of comparison of two absolutes, either in reality or in thought, that is, in the reasoning of the mind. And this one ratio is nothing other than one underlying accident, composed of two accidents which befall two absolute and separate things.

units.la: Est autem categoria relatorum ὁμώνυμος propter diuersa subiecta. Interdum enim res ab-soluta, interdum etiā res relata significatur. Mos dicitur maior: non quia maior per se fit: sed quia particeps est quantitatis & exuperantiae cuiusdam. Sic scientia relatum dicitur, nō ea ratione, qua est qualitas quaedam, sed qua mensuratum quiddam. Res autem relata significatur, ut cùm dicimus duplum esse dimidii duplum. Idcirco etiam Aristoteles duo genera relatorum ponit: unum genus illorum, quae ipsa quidquid sunt, a-liorum esse dicuntur. Sic duplum quidquid est, dimidii duplum esse dicitur. Alterum genus est illorum, quae quocunque modo alio ad alterum referuntur, quae nimirū propter διορισμὸν[?] quen dam ad alterum referuntur: ut montem ad mon tem referri diximus, propter exuperantiam, qua superat alterum montem.
units.tr: Now the category of relatives is homonymous on account of the different subjects. For sometimes an absolute thing is signified, and sometimes also a related thing. A greater is so called not because it becomes greater in itself, but because it shares in a certain quantity and excess. Thus knowledge is called a relative, not in the sense in which it is a certain quality, but in the sense in which it is something measured. A related thing is signified, for instance when we say that the double is the double of the half. Hence Aristotle also posits two kinds of relatives: one kind, of those which, whatever they are, are said to be of others. Thus whatever the double is, it is said to be the double of the half. The other kind is of those which are referred to another in whatever way, which indeed are referred to one another on account of a certain distinction: as we said a mountain is referred to a mountain on account of the excess by which one mountain surpasses the other.

units.la: Sed ut relatorum naturam accuratius expen-damus, tria relatorum constituenda sunt genera.
units.tr: But that we may weigh the nature of relatives more accurately, three kinds of relatives must be established.

units.la: Primùm genus,relationes numerorum,item ex-latorum vperantias ad exuperatum continet: & proinde ad hoc genus reuocantur omnes proportiones & relata secundùm maius seu plus & minus. Ex his Mathematicus illas dūtaxat comparationes & relationes cōsiderat, quæ speciē quadam proportionis definiri possunt. Nam quæ sunt infinita, qualia sunt καθ᾽ ἕκαστα[?] accidentia, in scientias non veniunt, sed sensu duntaxat percipiuntur: vt si quis maius & minus, exuperàs & exuperatum sensu duntaxat percipiat, nec sub specie aliqua numeri paris aut imparis, aut proportionis, aut æqualis aut inæqualis, comprehendat. Quæ igitur actu comparari possunt quantitates, ad speciem quandam καθ᾽ ὅλα[?] referuntur. Quædā sunt quæ licet non actu, δυνάμει[?] tamen sunt comparabiles: vt est διπλασίων[?] cum latere sui quadrati. Quæ vero nec actu nec δυνάμει sunt comparabiles, sunt ἄλογοι, id est, rationis seu relationis & comparationis expertes. Atq; hæc de primo genere relatorum, quod proprie ad quantitatem pertinet.
units.tr: The first kind contains the relations of numbers, and likewise the excesses of the greater to the exceeded; and therefore all proportions and relations according to greater or more and less are reduced to this kind. From these the mathematician considers only those comparisons and relations which can be defined under some species of proportion. For those which are infinite, such as the particular accidents (kath' hekasta), do not enter into the sciences, but are perceived by the sense alone: as when someone perceives the greater and less, the excess and the exceeded, by sense alone, and does not comprehend them under any species of number, even or odd, or of proportion, or of equal or unequal. Therefore quantities which can actually be compared are referred to a certain species according to wholes. Some are such that, although not actually, yet potentially they are comparable: as the double is with the side of its square. But those which are comparable neither actually nor potentially are irrational (alogoi), that is, lacking reason, relation, and comparison. And so much for the first kind of relatives, which properly pertains to quantity.

units.la: Secundū genus relatorum complectitur efficiens & id quod fit: quod fecit & quod factū est: quod efficiet & quod fiet: denique agens & patiens. Aristoteles ait hæc dici πρός τι τῷ δυνα-μικῷ καὶ παθητικῷ. In hoc genere considerantur ἐνέργεια & δυνάμεις ποιητικαὶ καὶ παθητικαί: in priore vero non considerātur. Exemplum Aristotelis est Θερμαντὸν καὶ Θερμαντικόν, & Θερμαινόμενον καὶ Θερμαινόμενον: illud ὅτι δύναται: hoc ὅτι ἐνεργεῖ[?]. Illa verò à quibus denominantur agentia aut patientia, non sunt in eadem categoria: vt actio & passio, à quibus denominantur agens & patiens.
units.tr: The second kind of relatives comprises the efficient and that which is made: what made and what has been made: what will make and what will be made: finally the agent and the patient. Aristotle says these are called relative with respect to the active and the passive (pros ti tō dynamikō kai pathētikō). In this kind are considered the actions and the active and passive powers; but in the former they are not considered. Aristotle's example is "heating thing" and "heater", and "heated thing" and "heatable": the former in that it is able, the latter in that it is acting. But those things from which agents or patients are named are not in the same category, such as action and passion, from which the agent and the patient are named.

units.la: Tertium genus relatorum est eorum quæ re-feruntur, vt τὸ μετρητὸν πρὸς τὸ μέτρον[?]: aut διπλάσιον πρὸς ἡμίσειαν[?]. Res quæ dicitur μὴ τρίτη[?], non refertur per se: vt ager non refertur per se ad limitem, nisi quia est limitatus. In his relatis vnū est causa relationis alterius: & vnum est natura prius altero. Illúdque est veluti mensura alterius. Natura quidem, si prius est natura vt causa: nobis verò ratione nostræ cognitionis: vt effectum.
units.tr: The third kind of relatives is of those things which are referred to one another, such as the measurable in relation to the measure, or the double in relation to the half. A thing which is called "not third" (me tritē) is not referred of itself: for example a field is not referred of itself to a boundary, except because it is bounded. In these relatives one is the cause of the relation of the other, and one is prior by nature to the other. And the one is, as it were, the measure of the other. Prior by nature, indeed, if it is prior as cause; but for us, by reason of our knowledge, as effect.

units.la: Hæc relata nō possunt dici antequam vnum: vt mensura ad alterum vt μετρητὸν[?], adhibeatur. Nomen autem relationi accommodandum est, quale est μετρητὸν, διπλασιὸν[?] & cætera eiusmodi. Sed non semper quæ sunt ὅμοιο[?] τρίτῳ[?], sunt ipsa μετρητὰ[?]: nam nō raro ipsa sunt μέτρον[?]: vt ὅπερ ἔστιν[?], quod est natura prius scientia, est μέτρον seu mensura scientiæ. Persæpe quoque illud, quod nobis est mensura, est natura μετρητὸν: & contra, vt dictum est.
units.tr: These relatives cannot be spoken of before one of them is applied as measure to the other as measurable. A name suited to the relation must be given, such as measurable, double, and the like. But those things which are similar to a third are not always themselves measurables: for often they are themselves measures: as that which is prior by nature to science is the measure or standard of science. Very often also that which is a measure for us is the measurable by nature; and conversely, as has been said.

units.la: Ad hoc tertium genus Aristoteles hæc quatuor revocat, ἕξιν, θέσιν, διάθεσιν, & ὅπου ἡμῶν[?]. Ac ἕξις quidem hic significat habitionem potiùs, quàm habitū: quo modo dicit Aristoteles τὰ ἄντα τῷ ἔχειν ἐν αὐτῇ[?]. Quicquid enim est, aut subiectū est, & habet: aut est in subiecto, & habetur: vt forma dicitur haberi ratione subiecti ἕξις. vel materiæ, estque mensura:& est natura prius quiddam: subiectum vero quod habet, est mensuratum quoddam & natura posterius. Quæ enim habent, definiuntur per suas formas habitas. Θέσις situm seu locationé significat, qua referuntur locus & locatum: ac locus quidem mensura est locati, quia differentiæ locatorum naturis locorum intelliguntur. Sic leue definitur & intelligitur superno loco, & graue inferno. Sic θέσει intelligimus dextrum, sinistrum, pone, ante, & cætera eiusmodi. Διάθεσις, partium causa, ipsi toti accidit. Atqui ipsa διάθεσις seu dispositio partium est mensura disponens totum, & proinde totum hac mensura dispositum tanquam mensuratum dicitur. Σχῆσις & διαίρεσις species sunt διαθέσεως: sunt enim affectiones quædam partium, relpectu totius. Ἐπίσχεσις ad ἕξιν refertur eo modo, quo μέτρον ad μέτρον, & vnum est causa relationis alterius: neque enim ἐπίσχεσις refertur nisi ratione ἕξεως, ὅτι ὡς ἐκεῖνο, ὃ ἕξιν ἐπίσχεσις.
units.tr: To this third kind Aristotle reduces these four: having (hexis), position (thesis), disposition (diathesis), and where (hopou hēmōn). Here hexis signifies more a having than a habit: in the way Aristotle says that things are opposed in having something in them. For whatever exists either is a subject and has, or is in a subject and is had: as form is said to be had by reason of the subject, a hexis, or of the matter, and is a measure; and it is something prior by nature; but the subject which has it is something measured and posterior by nature. For those which have are defined through their forms as possessed. Thesis signifies position or location, by which place and the located are related; and place is indeed the measure of the located, because the differences of located things are understood by the natures of places. Thus the light is defined and understood by the upper place, and the heavy by the lower. Thus by thesis we understand right, left, behind, before, and other such things. Diathesis, which is a disposition of parts, belongs to the whole itself. Yet diathesis itself, or the disposition of parts, is a measure disposing the whole, and therefore the whole disposed by this measure is called as the measured. Schesis and diairesis are species of diathesis: for they are certain affections of parts with respect to the whole. Epischesis is referred to hexis in the way that measure is referred to measure, and one is the cause of the relation of the other: for epischesis is referred only by reason of hexis, in that as that is, so epischesis is.

units.la: Relatis Relatis, sed non omnibus, inest contrarietas: vt ἐπίσχεσις ἀγνοία, est contraria. At duplo nihil est contrarium, neque triplo.
units.tr: Some relatives, though not all, have contrariety: as ignorance is contrary to knowledge (epischesis agnoia). But nothing is contrary to double, nor to triple.

units.la: Præterea quædam relata videntur suscipere id quod est magis & minus. Nā simile & æquale, quæ sunt relata, dicuntur magis & minus. sed non omnia relata dicuntur magis & minus: nam duplum non dicitur magis & minus duplum.
units.tr: Moreover, certain relatives seem to admit the more and the less. For like and equal, which are relatives, are said to be more and less. But not all relatives are said to be more and less: for double is not said to be more or less double.

units.la: Commune est omnium relatorum reciprocè dici inter se: vt duplum dimidii duplum dicitur: efficiens eius quod fit efficiens: ἕτερον ἡμῶν τὸ ἕτε- ρον[?] ἕτερον ἡμῶν[?]. Nonnunquam verò correlati nomen non est expressum vlitata voce, quo fit vt ὀνομαξοποιεῖν[?] necesse sit, quæ ὀνομαξοποιά[?] habet locum in relatis tertii generis. Quòd si non rectè assignetur correlatum, nulla erit reciproca relatio. Exemplum proponit Aristot. in tertio genere relatorum re:clauus nō dicitur nauis clauus reciprocè, sed clauus clauati(vt ita dicam)clauus.
units.tr: It is common to all relatives to be said reciprocally to one another: as the double is said to be the double of the half; the efficient of what is made is the efficient [heteron hēmōn to heteron, heteron hēmōn]. Sometimes, however, the name of the correlate is not expressed by the usual word, whence it becomes necessary to coin a name (onomatopoiein), and this coining of names has its place in relatives of the third kind. But if the correlate is not rightly assigned, there will be no reciprocal relation. Aristotle gives an example in the third kind of relatives: the nail of a ship is not said reciprocally the ship's nail, but the nail of the nailed (as I may say) nail.

units.la: Primi præsertim & secundi generis plurima relata, cùm reciprocè afferuntur, retinent casum eundem: vt duplum dimidii duplū, & dimidium dupli dimidium. Sic τοιπικὸν τῆς παθητικοῦ[?] τοιπικὸν[?], & παθητικὸν τῆς τοιπικῆς[?]. Atteritii generis relata mutat casum: vt oculus oculi oculus: oculatum oculo oculatum.
units.tr: Most relata of the first and second kinds, when they are stated reciprocally, keep the same case: for example, double of half is double, and half of double is half. So the quality of the passive [τοιπικὸν τῆς παθητικοῦ] is quality [τοιπικὸν], and the passive [παθητικὸν] is of the qualitative [τῆς τοιπικῆς]. But relata of the third kind change their case: eye of the eye is eye, and eyed of eye is eyed.

units.la: Præterea relata videtur esse simul natura, ac in primis relata primi & secundi generis: tertii verò generis relata non videntur esse simul: nam ἔτερον[?] videtur natura esse prius ipsa scientia.
