Fieri enim potest vt aliquid sit ἕτερον[?], cuius tamen non sit vlla ἕτερον[?]: vt si τετραγωνισμὸν[?] circuli ἕτερον[?] esse ponamus, cuius tamen nulla est scientia. Et in quibus aliquid est φύσει[?] prius, illa simul natura nō esse videntur, quanuis sint λόγῳ[?] simul. Sunt autem priora natura: causa, ratione effecti: mensura ratione mensurati: & vnum ratione multorum.
units.tr: Moreover, relata seem to be simultaneous by nature, especially the relata of the first and second kinds. Relata of the third kind do not seem to be simultaneous, for [ἔτερον] seems to be prior by nature to knowledge itself. For it can happen that something is [ἕτερον], yet has no [ἕτερον] at all: for example, if we suppose the squaring of the circle to be [ἕτερον], of which there is nevertheless no knowledge. And in those things where one thing is prior [φύσει], they do not seem to be simultaneous by nature, although they are simultaneous [λόγῳ]. Things are prior by nature as follows: cause to effect, measure to measured by reason, and one to many by reason.

units.la: Cùm dicimus mensurā esse aliquid prius ipso mensurato, non sic accipiendum est, vt omnia nomina hunc in modum formata, sint mesurata: quum ex illis multa sint vt mensurae. Sic ἐπισή-τὸν ἐπιςήμης mensura & prius quid φύσει dici-tur. Quod autem ἐπιςήντὸν sit prius natura ipsa scientia, probat Ariftoteles eo, quòd sublatis ἐ-πιςήμης scietia esse non possit. At sublata fcien-tia possunt esse ipsa ἐπιςήντά: & sublato animali non erit scientia: & tamen poterunt esse multa ἐπιςήντά. Denique exemplo αἰσθήσεως & αἰ-σθητὰ probari potest, tertii generis relata non esse simul φύσει. Nam αἰσθητὰ fuerunt ante-quam esset αἰσθητικὸν: atqui αἴσθησις extitit ἅ-μα τῷ αἰσθητικῷ & non ante. Quare si αἰσθητὰ fuerunt antequam esset αἰσθητικὸν, fuerunt e-tiam ante αἴσθησιν. Ex quo efficitur, hæc relata non esse simul natura.
units.tr: When we say that a measure is something prior to what is measured, this must not be understood to mean that all names formed in this way are measured, since many of them are measures. Thus knowable [ἐπιςήντὸν] and knowledge are said to be measure and prior by nature. Aristotle proves that the knowable [ἐπιςήντὸν] is prior by nature to knowledge itself, because when knowledge is removed, it cannot exist. But when knowledge is removed, the knowables [ἐπιςήντά] themselves can exist; and when the animal is removed, there will be no knowledge, and yet there can be many knowables. Finally, by the example of sensation [αἰσθήσεως] and sensibles [αἰσθητὰ] it can be proved that relata of the third kind are not simultaneous by nature. For sensibles existed before the sensitive faculty [αἰσθητικὸν] existed; but sensation [αἴσθησις] came into being together with the sensitive faculty [ἅμα τῷ αἰσθητικῷ] and not before. Therefore, if the sensibles existed before the sensitive faculty existed, they also existed before sensation. From this it follows that these relata are not simultaneous by nature.

units.la: Quæritur vtrum substantia ipsa per fe resera-tur, id est, vtrum esse cuiufdam substantiæ, quia substantia, fit ad aliud referri. Substantia certè vi-detur esse absolutissima & χωρισὸν quiddam re-&ratione, & semet ipsa id quod est, esse: & pro-inde nō videtur relationibus subiici. Vt, animal non eo, quòd fit alterius, intelligitur: vt neq; ho-mo, neque Socrates. Partes verò fubftatiarum, quòd referuntur, id eis accidit, nō quia sunt sub-stantiæ, sed quia prædita sunt continua aut di-fcreta quantitate. Deinde quia denominatur ab aliis, & quasi mensurata quædā ratione aliorum intelligūtur: vt oculus quid fit intelligitur ra-tione animalis oculati: & sic oculus est tanquam mensuratum ab oculato. Hoc modo partes tan-quam relata à nobis cognoscuntur, idque qua-tenus, tenus, vt secundæ substātiæ cognoscūtur, nō aūt vt primæ. Neq; enim si quis ignotus per foramē proferat brachium, quid sit brachium possit aliter cognosci, aut intelligi, quàm ratione τῷ καθόλου[?]: vt neque occultati reliqui corporis oculus, vel pes potest nosci alia ratione, quàm energia sua, incognito illo ipso animali singulari cuius est. Cùm autem relata quæ verè relata dicuntur, non tantùm quatenus καθόλου, sed etiam & multò magis quatenus καθέκαστα quidquid sùt, id esse ratione aliorum noscantur, & vno cognito, simul alterum cognosci oportet: partes substantiarum in illis non numerabuntur, quia non possunt perfectè referri: erúntque potiùs in prædicamento substantiæ, quàm relationis, nisi quodammodo, seu ὁπωσοῦν[?] dicantur relata, ea nëpe ratione, qua sunt partes totius συνόλως[?], & men furata[?] quædam à toto.
units.tr: It is asked whether substance itself is referred through itself, that is, whether the being of a certain substance, because it is substance, is able to be referred to another. Substance certainly seems to be most absolute and something separate [χωρισὸν] in thought and reason, and to be what it is by itself; and therefore it does not seem to be subject to relations. Thus an animal is not understood through being of another, nor is a man, nor Socrates. But the parts of substances, insofar as they are referred, have this happen to them not because they are substances, but because they are endowed with continuous or discrete quantity. Then, because they are named from others and are understood as in some way measured by others: thus the eye is understood as what it is by reason of the eyed animal, and so the eye is as it were measured by the eyed. In this way parts are known by us as relata, and this insofar as they are known as secondary substances, not as primary ones. For if someone unknown were to put forward an arm through a hole, what an arm is could not be known or understood in any other way than by reason of the universal [τῷ καθόλου]; nor can the eye or foot of a hidden rest of the body be known by any other means than by its own function, the individual animal to which it belongs remaining unknown. But since relata which are truly called relata are known to be in relation to others not only insofar as they are universal [καθόλου], but also, and much more, insofar as they are particular [καθέκαστα], whatever they are, and since when one is known the other must be known at the same time, the parts of substances will not be counted among those, because they cannot be referred completely; and they will be placed rather in the category of substance than of relation, unless they are called relata in some way [ὁπωσοῦν], namely in the sense in which they are parts of a whole [συνόλως] and something measured in some way by the whole.

units.la: CATEGORIA QVALITATIS.
units.tr: CATEGORY OF QUALITY.

units.la: CAtegoria Qualitatis est ὁμώνυμος, vt quæ de diuersis primò generibus prædicetur, nō ex vna ratione & definitione. Qualitatis autem genera sunt hæc, διαθέσεις[?], quam dispositione vo cant: φυσικαὶ δυνάμεις seu ἀδυναμίαι id est, facultates seu potentiæ naturales & impotetiæ: qualitatis παθητικαὶ ποιότητες, quibus sensus externi afficiútur:figura & forma.Διάθεσις significat motu acquisitam qualitatem, éstq; vel μόνιμος, aut ἐυκίνητος, id est (vt ita dicam) durabilis vel non durabilis.Quæ est ἐυκίνητος nomen generis retinet:quæ vero est μόνιμος,ἕξις,id est,habitus dicitur. Potentiæ & materiæ causa mouentur res tantisper, dum ἐχέσιν[?] vel habitum cōsequutæ sint: est enim dispositio perfectio quædam, & multò magis ἕξις. Hinc etiam habitus dicitur qualitas,secundum quam res non facilè afficiuntur, aut habefactantur à cōtrario:vt sanitas,quatenus est ἕξις, non facilè afficitur à causis morbificis. Et morbus hecticus non facilè expugnatur remediis,imò non cedit contrariis remediis. Est autem magni momenti habitus in omnibus rebus: quia nisi esset habitus, omnia semper afficerentur,& ἀεὶ[?] πάθεια[?] daretur.Διάθεσις facilè à contrariis afficitur,quia nondum est confirmatus habitus. Ad hoc genus qualitatis nempe διαθέσεως[?] Galenus morbos omnes,causas morborum,& συμπτώματα[?] reuocauit.
units.tr: The category of Quality is homonymous, since it is predicated of diverse primary genera, not according to one account and definition. The genera of quality are these: disposition (which they call διάθεσις), natural powers or impotences (φυσικαὶ δυνάμεις or ἀδυναμίαι), that is, natural faculties or capacities and incapacities; passive qualities (παθητικαὶ ποιότητες), by which the external senses are affected; and figure and form. Διάθεσις signifies a quality acquired by motion, and it is either μόνιμος or ἐυκίνητος, that is (so to speak) durable or not durable. That which is ἐυκίνητος retains the name of the genus; but that which is μόνιμος is called ἕξις, that is, habit. Things are moved by potency and matter only so long as they have attained ἐχέσιν or habit, for disposition is a certain imperfection, and much more so is ἕξις. Hence a quality is also called a habit when things are not easily affected or dislodged by the contrary; thus health, insofar as it is ἕξις, is not easily affected by morbific causes. And hectic fever is not easily overcome by remedies, indeed it does not yield to contrary remedies. Habit is, moreover, of great importance in all things: for unless there were habit, all things would always be affected, and ἀεὶ πάθεια would be given. Disposition is easily affected by contraries, because the habit is not yet confirmed. To this genus of quality, namely disposition, Galen referred all diseases, causes of diseases, and symptoms (συμπτώματα).

units.la: Secundum genus qualitatis sunt δυνάμεις[?] φυσικαὶ (seu ἀδυναμίαι), quæ rebus ex materia & forma compositis insunt natura: síntq; actionis aut passionis cuiusdam principium. Alio modo dicuntur δυνάμεις partes illæ,quæ formam ipsam constituunt,quæ ὑπάρχουσι sunt, non accidentia: cuiusmodi sunt animæ δυνάμεις seu facultates. At δυνάμεις φυσικαὶ hic dicuntur propter quas ὑπάρχει naturales quasdam ἕξεις acquirere possunt vel non possunt: vt sunt inepti omnino ad artes, qui non possunt erudiri: alii vero ad virtutes & literas sunt aptiores. Galenus ait facultates & difficultates naturales eiusmodi, inesse subiectis propter temperamenta, quae quidem licet φύσεις nonnullis dicantur, nō sunt tamen ἀρχαὶ ὑποιωδεῖς[?] rerum. Denique varietatis in temperamentis materia, est causa. Vtautem variae sunt δυνάμεις & ἀδυναμίαι, seu εὐφυίαι καὶ ἀφυίαι ingeniorum & animorum, ita etiam corporum. Quædam enim corpora reperiuntur ὑγιεινά, quae non facile morbis succumbunt. Hæ δυνάμεις φυσικαὶ efficiunt vt facilius διαθέσεις & ἕξεις suscipiatur. Et quod aliquid potest fieri ex imperfecto perfectum, illud fit ratione φυσικῆς seu εὐφυτῆς δυνάμεως. Aristoteles exemplum δυνάμεως φυσικῆς in corporibus proponit, nempe duritiem, qua corpora non facile admittunt divisionem: ἀδυναμίας vero exemplum, mollitiem, qua corpora divisioni non possunt resistere. In hoc genere sunt qualitates illae, propter quas res coqui, assari, maturari, concrescere, findi, frangi, scindi, possunt.
units.tr: The second genus of quality is natural powers (φυσικαὶ δυνάμεις, or ἀδυναμίαι), which are inherent in things composed of matter and form by nature, and are the principle of some action or passion. In another sense, the powers are those parts which constitute the form itself, which are ὑπάρχουσι, not accidents; of this kind are the powers or faculties of the soul. But natural powers are here so called because, by means of them, a subject can or cannot acquire certain natural habits: for example, men who are wholly unfit for the arts, who cannot be taught, while others are more apt for virtues and letters. Galen says that such natural faculties and incapacities inhere in subjects on account of their temperaments, which, although some call them natures, are nevertheless not the ὑποιωδεῖς principles of things. Finally, the matter of the temperaments is the cause of variety. And just as there are various powers and incapacities, or εὐφυίαι and ἀφυίαι, of talents and minds, so also are there of bodies. For some bodies are found to be ὑγιεινά, which do not easily succumb to diseases. These natural powers bring it about that dispositions and habits are more readily acquired. And whatever can be made perfect from the imperfect, this comes about by reason of a natural or well-born power. Aristotle offers as an example of a natural power in bodies hardness, by which bodies do not readily admit division; but as an example of incapacity, softness, by which bodies cannot resist division. In this genus are those qualities on account of which things can be cooked, roasted, ripened, congealed, split, broken, and cut.

units.la: Tertium genus παθητικαὶ ποιότητες[?] con-stituunt: quae παθητικαί[?] dicuntur, non quod res naturales[?] propter has qualitates misceantur, tem-perentúrque inter se: sed quòd sensus his pro-prie afficiantur. Sunt autem quinque numero, quibus per se sensus externi assi-ciuntur: color, sonus, odor, sapor, tactilis qualitas. Ex his solæ tactiles qualitates primæ, nempe calidū, frigidum, humidum, siccum, extra sensum mutuis actionibus & perpessionibus sese afficiunt: sed cùm hūc in modum miscentur & temperantur calidum, frigidum, humidum, & siccum non dicuntur <bl>πρῶτα θερμικαὶ ποιότητες</bl>, sed <bl>πάσχειν</bl> dicuntur, vt di cemus. Porrò cauendum est ne hoc qualitatum genus cum praecedenti confundamus. Non con fundemus, si ex eo dūtaxat <bl>φυσικὰς δυνάμεις</bl> consideremus, quòd perfici habitibus possint: esse con- qualitates verò <bl>παθητικὰς</bl>, ex eo quòd proprie sensus afficiant. Etsi enim in hoc & in illo genere videatur inesse <bl>δύναμις ποιητικὴ</bl>: tamen <bl>δύναμις</bl> hæc <bl>ποιητικὴ ὁμωνύμως</bl> de vtroq; ge-nere dicitur. Iccirco etiam Aristoteles maluit <bl>παθητικὰς ποιότητας</bl> has appellare, sic vt intelligeremus qualitates <bl>ποιητικὰς τῶ πάθους</bl> in sensibus. Qualitates quoque <bl>παθητικαὶ</bl> dicuntur, nō <bl>ποιητικαὶ τῶ πάθους</bl>, sed <bl>τῷ αὐτὸς ὑπὸ πάθους γεγονέναι</bl>, id est, eo quod ex perpessione existant, nō qualibet, sed quæ sint <bl>δυσκίνητος</bl>: ideo <bl>παρὰ τὸ πάθος παθητικὰ</bl> rectè videntur dici: quæ tamen re vera dicuntur etiam <bl>παθητικαὶ ποιότητες</bl>, eo quod sensus afficiāt. Neque enim vllam habent vim <bl>ἐνεργητικὴν</bl> præterquam ratione sensuum. Ipsum autem <bl>πάθος</bl> quod est <bl>δυσκίνητον</bl> habet plerūq; causam constitutionem quandam naturalem: estque veluti <bl>ἡρᾶσις</bl>. Sic multi ex constitutione quadam naturali sunt candidi aut nigri. Quod si <bl>πάθος</bl> eiusmodi sit, quod excitatum, subitò euanescat, non ad <bl>παθητικὴν ποιότητα</bl>, sed ad categoriam <bl>τὸ πάσχειν</bl> reuocari debet. Vt si quis pudore fufsus erubes at. Vt autem qualitates hæ παθη-τικὰ dicun[?]ur, eo quod sensus afficiantur: ita etiā παθητικαὶ ποιότητες dici possunt, iracundia, velan[?]a, voluptas: eo quod his animus alicuius affici soleat.
units.tr: The third genus constitutes the passive qualities (παθητικαὶ ποιότητες). They are called passive, not because natural things are mixed or tempered with one another by these qualities, but because the senses are properly affected by them. There are five of them, by which the external senses are affected of themselves: colour, sound, odour, flavour, and tactile quality. Of these, only the primary tactile qualities, namely hot, cold, moist, and dry, affect one another by mutual actions and passions outside the sense; but when hot, cold, moist, and dry are mixed and tempered in this way, they are not called πρῶτα θερμικαὶ ποιότητες, but are said to be πάσχειν, as we shall say. Moreover, we must take care not to confuse this genus of quality with the preceding one. We shall not confuse them if we consider these only as natural powers, because they can be perfected by habits, but as passive qualities, because they properly affect the senses. For although a active power (δύναμις ποιητικὴ) seems to be present in both this and that genus, nevertheless this active power is predicated homonymously of both genera. Therefore Aristotle also preferred to call these παθητικὰς ποιότητας, so that we might understand them as qualities that make an impression (ποιητικὰς τῶ πάθους) upon the senses. Qualities are also called passive, not ποιητικαὶ τῶ πάθους, but τῷ αὐτὸς ὑπὸ πάθους γεγονέναι, that is, because they come into existence from a passion; not any passion, but one that is δυσκίνητος; therefore it seems rightly said that they are παρὰ τὸ πάθος παθητικά; yet in truth they are also called παθητικαὶ ποιότητες, because they affect the senses. For they have no ἐνεργητικὴν power except by reason of the senses. But the passion itself, which is δυσκίνητον, usually has as its cause a certain natural constitution, and is as it were an ἡρᾶσις. Thus many people are white or black from a certain natural constitution. But if the passion is of such a kind that, once excited, it quickly vanishes, it must be referred not to the passive quality but to the category of τὸ πάσχειν; as when someone, suffused with shame, blushes. And just as these qualities are called παθητικά because they affect the senses, so also they may be called παθητικαὶ ποιότητες: anger, sorrow, pleasure, because the mind of someone is wont to be affected by these.

units.la: Quartum genus qualitatis est, Figura & Forma: at figura quidem, ut est qualitas quaedam determinans superficiem corporis, non ut ipsa superficies: hoc est, ut est qualitas, non ut quantitas hic intelligitur. Hinc etiam qua παρωνύμως praedicantur à figura, ut qualitates[?] in eadem sunt categoria, atque ipsa figura. Sic rectum & curvum παρωνύμως praedicantur de subiecto ut sunt differentiae qualitatis, non autem quantitatis. Sic rotundū de ligno, aut lapide. Forma quo-que non ut forma ἁπλῶς[?] dicta, sed ut materiata, hoc est, ut facta ex materia quadā, intelligenda est: quam Aristoteles τῷ ἐν τῷ αἰσθητῷ[?] μορφῷ appellat. Sic mensa dicitur lignea materia causa, quae figuram mensae talem reddit, nempe ligneam. Sic triangulum ligneum. Domus lapidea. Ipsa autem materia talis dicitur, quia est figura quaedam praedita: ut lignum curvum, lapis rotundus. Ex his intelligitur materiā praedicari παρωνύμως de figura: & determinare quodammodo figuram, non ex sua natura (est enim ἀόριστος[?]) sed quia μορφὴν[?] quandam habet: & propter materiam figuras & formas considerari ut qualitatum genera: à quibus res paronymae dicantur tales. Figurarum quoq; nomina esse homo-nyma sciendum est. Nam cùm ita definiuntur, vt quatitas quædam exprimatur, ad categoriam quantitatis reuocantur. Quū vero qualitas quædam corporis & non quantitas exprimitur, ad hoc quartum genus qualitatis referuntur.
units.tr: The fourth genus of quality is figure and form. Figure, indeed, as it is a certain quality determining the surface of a body, not as the surface itself; that is, it is understood here as a quality, not as a quantity. Hence also those things which are predicated paronymously from figure, as qualities, are in the same category as figure itself. Thus straight and curved are predicated paronymously of a subject as differences of quality, not of quantity. So round is said of wood or stone. Form too must be understood not as form taken absolutely, but as embodied, that is, as made from a certain matter, which Aristotle calls the form in the sensible (τῷ ἐν τῷ αἰσθητῷ μορφῷ). So a table is called wooden by reason of its matter, which makes the figure of the table such, namely wooden. So a wooden triangle; a stone house. But matter itself is said to be such because it is endowed with a certain figure: as a curved wood, a round stone. From these things it is understood that matter is predicated paronymously of figure, and in some way determines the figure, not by its own nature (for it is ἀόριστος), but because it has a certain form; and on account of the matter, figures and forms are considered as genera of qualities, from which things are called paronymous as such. It must also be known that the names of figures are homonymous. For when they are defined so as to express a certain quantity, they are referred to the category of quantity; but when a certain quality of a body, and not quantity, is expressed, they are referred to this fourth genus of quality.

units.la: Cæterùm non videntur esse alia quædam genera qualitatis. Quanuis enim rarum, densum, asperum & læue, videantur esse qualitates, quia παρωνύμως prædicantur: tamen nō sunt ad qualitatem, sed ad relationem referenda. Nam non alia ratione intelliguntur quid sint, quàm διέσει quædam partium. Διέσις autem est in genere τῶν πρός τι: liquidem διέσις partium relatione ad totum noscitur. Sic dicitur rarum, totum quid: cuius partes (ratione materiæ) sunt dilatatæ. Densum, totum quid, cuius partes sunt propius arctiúsque coniunctæ & quasi coactæ. Læue & politum, cuius tota planities ratione partium, est æquabilis. Asperum contrà, cuius partes sunt inæquales depressione & eminentia.
units.tr: Moreover, there do not seem to be any other genera of quality. For although rare, dense, rough and smooth seem to be qualities, because they are predicated paronymously, nevertheless they are not to be referred to quality but to relation. For they are not understood in any other way than as a certain disposition of parts. Now διέσις is in the genus of τῶν πρός τι (relatives): for the διέσις of parts is known by relation to the whole. Thus the rare is said of a whole thing whose parts are (by reason of matter) dilated. Dense: a whole thing whose parts are nearer and more tightly joined and as it were compressed. Smooth and polished: whose whole plane is even by reason of its parts. Rough, on the contrary: whose parts are unequal in depression and elevation.

units.la: Differentiæ verò generum: τὰ καθόλου νοη-τά: item propria, quanuis significent τοιόν δέ: tamen differentiæ ad categoriam generum: τὰ καθόλου νοητά ad categoriam illorum, de quibus in quid prædicatur: propria ἀντιφέροντα ad categoriam sui subiecti, reuocantur.
units.tr: But the differences of genera (τὰ καθόλου νοητά), likewise the properties, although they signify τοιόν δέ, nevertheless, differences are referred to the category of genera (τὰ καθόλου νοητά) and to the category of those things predicated in what-it-is, and properties (ἀντιφέροντα) are referred to the category of their subject.

units.la: Quæ generibus illis quatuor qualitatis subiiciuntur, qualitates sunt: secùndùm quas, res qualitatum in les, seu subiecta qualia dici cōsueuerūt. Hinc fit etiam vt παρωνύμως de subiectis prædicentur. Sed in omnibus non est eadē ratio παρωνυμίας.
units.tr: Those things which are subordinated to these four genera of quality are qualities, according to which things, or subjects, are said to be qualitative, or qualia, as they are customarily called. Hence it also comes about that they are predicated paronymously of subjects. But in all things the reason of paronymy is not the same.

units.la: eadem. paronymum(quod concretum vulgò dicitur) v-sitata sunt: ut albedo, album: iustitia, iustum. Alia sunt, quorum paronyma quidē sunt vsitata, sed non ipsa abstracta. Vt cùm à facultate naturali aliquis δ᾿ ἐργμικὸς[?] vel πυκτικὸς dicitur. Nomen enim iplius facultatis naturalis non est vsi-tatum. Artibus quidem quibus excoluntur,& quasi perficiuntur facultates ipsæ naturales, impositæ sunt nomina, cuiusmodi sunt πυκτικὴ, ἰατρικὴ: sed facultates ipsæ naturales certis non exprimuntur vocibus vsitatis, vt nec φυσικαὶ ἀρεταί, quibus apti homines dicuntur, vt habitibus ethicis informari possint. Aliorum abstractum seu synonymum est quidem vsitatum, sed paronymon non est: vt à virtute non denominatur virtuosus. Adhæc notandum est quorundam synonyma nō esse in categoria παρωνύμων suorum: vt lignū est in categoria substantiæ: ligneū verò in categoria qualitatis. Figura verò est vox homonymos. definitur enim aliquādo vt superficies seu quantitas: interdum verò vt qualitas. Quare figuratum, quod est paronymum, adhibita distinctione in eadem categoria cum suo synonymo esse dicendum est.
units.tr: The same applies to the paronym (what is commonly called the concrete): these are in common use, as whiteness and white, justice and just. Other terms have paronyms that are in common use, but not the abstract nouns themselves. For example, when someone is called a wrestler or a boxer from a natural faculty, the name of the natural faculty itself is not in use. Indeed, names have been given to the arts by which the natural faculties themselves are cultivated and, as it were, perfected, such as boxing and medicine; but the natural faculties themselves are not expressed by any established words, nor are the natural virtues, by which men are said to be apt, so that they can be shaped by ethical habits. Some abstract nouns or synonyms are in use, but have no paronym: for example, the virtuous is not named from virtue. Furthermore, it should be noted that some synonyms do not belong to the category of their paronyms: wood is in the category of substance, but wooden is in the category of quality. The figure, however, is a homonymous term: it is sometimes defined as a surface or a quantity, and at other times as a quality. Hence the figured, which is a paronym, must, with the distinction made, be said to be in the same category as its synonym.

units.la: Præterea in qualitate contrarietas inest. Sic iustitia & iniustitia: album & nigrum contraria dicuntur. Hinc, propter qualitates contrarias, ipsa etiam concreta contraria dicuntur. Sic albū cor nigro corpori contrarium dicitur, propter qualitates contrarias. Et si vnum contrariorum, est qualitas, alterum quoque est qualitas. Contraria omnino sub eodem genere sunt, vt album & nigrum sub colore. Quae vero sunt μεταξύ (vt colores inter album & nigrum medium) non dicuntur contraria, sed ex contrariis σύνθετα[?]. Ex quo etiam intelligitur non omnia ποιὰ[?] esse contraria.
units.tr: Furthermore, all those qualities on account of which natural things are mobile admit of more and less. For every motion occurs from one contrary to another through a middle. Thus what is moved from the warm to the cold becomes less warm and more cold. Those things that have no middle cannot be distinguished by degrees of motion, and therefore do not admit of more and less. Finally, those that have no contrary cannot be said to be more or less. Thus a circle is not more a circle than another circle. Synonyms, or abstracts, also do not admit of more and less, but their paronyms do: whiteness is not said to be more or less whiteness, but a white thing is said to be whiter than another.

units.la: Porrò qualitates omnes illae, propter quas res naturales sunt mobiles, suscipiunt ut quod est magis & minus. Omnis enim motus fit ex contrario in contrarium per medium. Sic quod ex calido movetur in frigidum, minus fit calidum & magis frigidum. Quae medium non habent, distinguuntur gradibus motionis non possunt, & proinde non suscipiunt magis & minus. Denique quae contrarium non habent, non possunt dici magis & minus. Sic circulus non est magis circulus altero circulo. Synonyma quoque seu abstracta non suscipiunt magis & minus, sed ipsa paronyma: ut albedo non dicitur magis & minus albedo, sed album altero magis album dicitur.
units.tr: It is, moreover, a property of qualities in the first place that things are called similar or dissimilar on account of them. And indeed quantities themselves are called similar and dissimilar to one another for no other reason than on account of qualities. Thus we also say similarly with the remaining genera, as with similar actions or passions; likewise, to be able or not to be able similarly. For in all genera, by reason of quality, analogical similarity can have a place.

units.la: Est autem in primis proprium qualitatum, vt propter eas res similes aut dissimiles dicatur. Adeoque ipsae quantitates, non aliam ob causam, quam propter qualitates, similes & dissimiles inter se dicuntur. Sic etiam reliqua genera vt cum similes actiones aut passiones: item similiter posse esse aut non, similiter dicimus. In omnibus enim generibus, causa qualitatis, analogica similitudo potest locum habere.
units.tr: It is especially proper to qualities that things are called similar or dissimilar on account of them. Indeed, quantities themselves are called similar and dissimilar to one another for no other reason than on account of qualities. So too with the remaining genera: we say that actions or passions are similar, and likewise that things can or cannot be similarly. For in all genera, analogical similarity can take place on account of quality.

units.la: Neq; est quod turbetur aliquis eo, quòd multa genera qualitatis videantur esse relata: cuiuf-modi sunt ἐπιστήμη, ἕξις, & διάθεσις, de quibus dictum est in categoria τῶν πρός τι. Horum e- enim genus species nō sunt πρός τι: vt scien-tia, quanuis sit πρός τι, tamen grammatica non πρός est πρός τι, quia est species. genus enim persæpe τι, quo-est homonymum & propter homonymiam, res diuersarū categoriarum significat. At si species ἄτομος esset πρός τι: necessariò quoque genus ζῷοι esset πρός τι. Cùm autem quales dicamur secun-dùm qualitates τὰς ποιότητας: & hæ qualita-tes non sint πρός τι: sequitur qualitates, secun-dùm quas dicimur quales, nō esse πρός τι. Quod τι. satis est ad ostendendum necessitatem huius categoriæ.
units.tr: Nor should anyone be disturbed by the fact that many kinds of quality seem to be relative: such as knowledge (ἐπιστήμη), habit (ἕξις), and disposition (διάθεσις), which were discussed in the category of relatives (τῶν πρός τι). For their genus is not a relative, though the species are: knowledge, although it is relative, is not so as a genus, but as a species. Grammar, for instance, is a species of knowledge, and the genus is not a relative in the same way that its species is. For the genus is often a τι, which is homonymous, and on account of this homonymy signifies things of different categories. But if the species were a relative, such as the individual (ἄτομος), the genus animal (ζῷον) would necessarily also be a relative. Since, however, we are called qualified according to the qualities (τὰς ποιότητας), and these qualities are not relatives, it follows that the qualities according to which we are called qualified are not relatives. This is enough to show the necessity of this category.

units.la: AGERE ET PATI, SEV Actio & Passio.
units.tr: ACTING AND SUFFERING, OR Action and Passion.

units.la: Quatuor illa categoriarum genera præcipua sunt: quæ sequūtur, sine mentione superio-rum non possunt explicari. Ac primùm quid sit categoria actio & passio, absque agente & patiente non potest intelligi. Quanuis autem diuersæ sint categoriæ actionis & passionis: tamen simul sunt exponendæ: quia, vt agentis & patientis vna est re-latio: ita etiā actionis & passionis vna est ad nu-merū energia, quæ, quia ratione est gemina (λό-γῳ enim seu ratione discernitur energia agentis ab energia patientis) sic vt vna de altera nō pospossit prædicari, necessario duo constituuntur prædicamenta diuersa actionis & passionis.
units.tr: These four genera of categories are the principal ones, and what follows cannot be explained without mention of the preceding ones. And first, what the category of action and passion is cannot be understood without an agent and a patient. Although the categories of action and passion are distinct, they must nevertheless be expounded together: because, just as there is one relation of agent and patient, so too there is one energy relating to the same thing for action and passion. Since this energy is twofold in its account (for the energy of the agent is distinguished from the energy of the patient by reason or account), so that one cannot be predicated of the other, two distinct categories of action and passion are necessarily constituted.

units.la: Est autem actio, ἐνέργεια perfecta ἢ ἐντε-λής, vt ab agente proficiscitur: neque per se di-uidua est partibus temporis, sic vt prior à posteriore differat. Passio vero est ἐνέργεια ἀτελής, quæ per se diuidua est partibus temporis, sic vt posterior perfectione differat à priore. Omnis autem motus passio est, quam sequitur quidam effectus, qui tanquam finis est, propter quem res mouebatur. Quare actio perficit subiectum: passio vero & motus sine quodam perficiuntur. Ac propter materiā, proprie res sunt patibiles, non autem ποιητικόν. Materia enim per se nullā vim habet ad agendum. Nonnunquam verò vocabula ἐνεργείας vtriusque, hoc est, actionis & passionis homonyma: vt nutricatio, interdum significat actum animæ, interdum verò πάθος corporis nutriti. Et in Theologia, iustificatio significat Dei iustificantis ἐνέργειαν, & iustificati hominis πάθος. Interdum etiam dubium est in quibusdam, vtrum πάθη sint nuncupanda, an verò actiones. Sensio enim videtur esse actio & ἐνέργεια: videtur etiam πάθος esse, sed quod πάθος videtur esse, id fit ratione exterioris organi, quod ab obiecto exuperante corrumpitur: ratione verò τῆς κοινῆς αἰσθήσεως, sensus non est πάθος, sed ἐνέργεια. Ad hæc animorum perturbationes, & motus, πάθη dicuntur: quæ πάθη si sunt δυ-σ[illegible, ~7 letters], vt qualitates considerantur, à quibus denominantur homines: vt ab iracundia, iracundus.
units.tr: Action is a perfect or complete energy (ἐνέργεια τελεία ἢ ἐντελής), as it proceeds from the agent, and it is not in itself divisible into parts of time, so that the earlier differs from the later. Passion, however, is an incomplete energy (ἐνέργεια ἀτελής), which is in itself divisible into parts of time, so that the later differs from the earlier in perfection. Every motion is a passion, which is followed by a certain effect, which is as it were the end, on account of which the thing was moved. Hence action perfects the subject, but passion and motion are perfected without some such thing. And on account of matter, things are properly patible, but not active (ποιητικόν). For matter by itself has no power to act. Sometimes, however, the words of both energies, that is, of action and passion, are homonyms: for example, nutrition sometimes signifies the act of the soul, and sometimes the passion (πάθος) of the nourished body. And in theology, justification signifies the energy (ἐνέργεια) of God justifying, and the passion (πάθος) of the justified man. Sometimes too it is doubtful in some cases whether they should be called passions or actions. For sensation seems to be an action and energy; it also seems to be a passion, but what seems to be a passion happens by reason of the external organ, which is corrupted by an overpowering object; but by reason of the common sense (τῆς κοινῆς αἰσθήσεως), sensation is not a passion but an energy. Moreover, the disturbances and motions of the minds are called passions (πάθη); and if these passions are bad (δυσ[illegible]), they are considered as qualities, from which men are named, as the wrathful from wrath.

units.la: Cæterùm agens quidem' & patiens sunt τῶν πρός τι:at ἐνέργειαι, quæ sunt fundamentum & terminus relatorum, categorias duas constituunt. Quare actio agentis est absolutum quiddam, & passio patientis. Neq; verò omnes ἐνέργειαι seu & passiones sunt coniunctæ cum passionibus. Sunt enim quædã ἐνέργειαι seu actiones, quæ sine motu existunt, & ipsæ sibi fines sunt: quales sunt videre, audire, θεωρεῖν. Ac harum ἐνεργειῶν cōcreta seu paronyma in eadem sunt categoria, atque ἐνέργειαι ipsæ. Sic sentiens est eiusdem categoriæ cum sensione. Aliarum actionum quæ coniunctæ sunt cum passionibus, cōcreta seu paronyma in alio prædicamento: sic agens & patiens sunt in categoria τῶν πρός τι.
units.tr: Furthermore, the agent and the patient are indeed relatives (τῶν πρός τι), but the energies, which are the foundation and terminus of relatives, constitute two categories. Hence the action of the agent is something absolute, and so is the passion of the patient. Nor, indeed, are all energies or passions connected with passions. For there are some energies or actions which exist without motion and are ends in themselves: such as seeing, hearing, and contemplating (θεωρεῖν). And the concretes or paronyms of these energies are in the same category as the energies themselves: thus the one who perceives is in the same category as perception. Of the other actions which are connected with passions, the concretes or paronyms are in another category: thus the agent and the patient are in the category of relatives (τῶν πρός τι).

units.la: Actioni etiam & passioni accidit: ut propter eas aliquid magis & minus facere aut fieri dica- tur. Nam magis & minus calefacere licet, item calefieri.
units.tr: It also belongs to action and passion that things are said to do or undergo more or less on account of them. For one may heat more or less, and likewise be heated.

units.la: Actio & passio seu agere & pati contrarieta- tem suscipiūt: calefacere enim & frigefacere sunt contraria: sic calefieri & frigefieri.
units.tr: Action and passion, or to act and to suffer, admit of contrariety: for to heat and to cool are contraries; so too to be heated and to be cooled.

units.la: Categoria Aliquando.
units.tr: Category: Sometime (Aliquando).

units.la: Genus hoc aliquādo sine tempore nosci non potest. Quod enim definitur certo tempore, di- citur esse aliquando. Atque in hoc genere conti nentur omnia prædicata rerū, quoad sunt in tem pore: ut hodie, heri, cras, perendie, calēdæ, idus, nonæ, olim iam, dudum. Item quæ sic efferun- tur: ut, tempore belli Gallici, anno quo Christus natus est. Denique illa, in quibus temporis, aut partium temporis fit mentio: ut mane, vesperi. Ex quibus intelligitur aliquando non esse ἀπλῶς (esset enim quantitas) sed esse genus quod praedicatur de re, quae continetur tempore.
units.tr: This genus cannot be known without time. For what is defined by a certain time is said to be "sometime." And in this genus are contained all the predicates of things insofar as they are in time: such as today, yesterday, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, the Kalends, Ides, Nones, long ago, a little while ago. Likewise those expressed thus: in the time of the Gallic war, in the year in which Christ was born. Finally, those in which mention is made of a time or part of a time: such as in the morning, in the evening. From these it is understood that "sometime" is not absolutely (for that would be quantity) but is a genus that is predicated of a thing which is contained in time.

units.la: Categoria Alicubi.
units.tr: Category: Somewhere (Alicubi).

units.la: Vt aliquando non est tempus, sed est genus determinans rem, quae continetur tempore: ita etiam Alicubi non est locus: sed est, loco quodam determinatum esse. Ac locus quidem est quantitas: alicubi vero continentis corporis ratione exprimitur. Sic superum, inferum, in medio esse, dicuntur alicubi.
units.tr: As "sometime" is not time, but a genus determining a thing that is contained in time, so also "somewhere" is not place, but is being determined to be in a certain place. And place indeed is quantity; but "somewhere" is expressed by reference to the containing body. Thus being above, below, or in the middle are said to be "somewhere."

units.la: Categoria, qua aliquid dicitur positum esse.
units.tr: Category by which something is said to be placed.

units.la: Θέσις est in categoria τῶν πρός τι, ut dictum est. Significat enim quandam partium relationem, quae ratione totius intelligitur: cuiusmodi sunt prona, supina Θέσις. At παρώνυμα quae [?]τῆς θέσεως dicuntur & ἀπὸ τῆς θέσεως, dicuntur & a speciebus Θέσεως, accidentia sunt absoluta, quae ad hanc categoriam reuocanda sunt: ut sedere, stare, rectum esse: tri-no, quadrato, aspectu, aut opposito distare: ad Orientem ad Occidentem esse situm.
units.tr: Position (θέσις) is in the category of relatives, as has been said. For it signifies a certain relation of parts, which is understood by reference to the whole: such as position as lying prone or supine. But the paronyms which are called from position (τῆς θέσεως) and from position (ἀπὸ τῆς θέσεως), and are also called from the species of position, are absolute accidents, which must be referred back to this category: such as to sit, to stand, to be upright; to be distant by three cubits, by a square, by an aspect, or by an opposition; to be situated toward the East, toward the West.

units.la: Categoria Habere.
units.tr: Category: Having (Habere).

units.la: Habere ὁμωνύμως dicitur, qua ratione in multis praedicamentis locum habet: ut si interpretemur album quod habet albedinem, aut scientem qui habet scientiam: bicubitum quod habet longitudinem duorum cubitorum. At hic Habere est genus Categoriae absolutum, quod non intelligitur absque mentione rei habitae, quatenus habetur ab aliquo: & παρωνύμως dicitur ab habi-tione tione, de qua in categoria τῶν πρός τι, sub nomine ἕξεως. Sic armatum esse, eti habere arma. Hæredem esse, hoc est, habere hæreditatem: vestitu esse, hoc est, habere vestem. Res vero quæ habetur, & is qui habet ad hanc categoriam non pertinent: vt vestis, & qui habet vestem. Ac habes quidem ad rem, quæ habetur, refertur vt n[?] en-sura ad mensuratum. Quare ad tertium genus relatorum referre par est.
units.tr: "To have" is said homonymously, in which sense it finds a place in many predicaments: as when we interpret "white" as that which has whiteness, or "knowing" as one who has knowledge, or "two-cubits-long" as that which has a length of two cubits. But here "to have" is an absolute genus of the category, which is not understood without mention of the thing had, insofar as it is held by someone; and it is said paronymously from the having, which is discussed in the category of relatives under the name of habit (ἕξις). Thus, to be armed is to have arms; to be an heir is to have an inheritance; to be clothed is to have a garment. But the thing which is had, and the one who has it, do not belong to this category, such as a garment and the one who has a garment. Indeed, "having" is related to the thing had as a measure is to the thing measured. Wherefore it is fitting to refer it to the third kind of relatives.

units.la: ΤᾺ ΜΕΤᾺ ΤᾺΣ ΚΑΤΗΓΟ-ρίας non esse prætermittenda.
units.tr: That the things after the categories are not to be passed over.

units.la: QVI Categorias tolli volunt è Dialectica, eo etiam argumento utûtur, quòd τὰ μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας nullo modo ad Dialecticum pertineant. Neque enim, aiunt, Dialectici est agere de oppositis de contrariis: multò minùs de motu, cuius consideratio ad Physicum pertinet. Quoniam igitur sublatis τῆς μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας, tolli etiam categorias volunt: si licet ponere categorias: τὰ μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας etiā ponere licebit. Atqui nos euicimus ponēdas esse categorias ex lege κατὰ παντὸς & καθ' αὐτό. Quod verò de motu afferût, speciosum quidē est, sed tamen falsum, Dialecticum nullo modo debere de motu agere in categoriis. Nam si de contrario, etiam de motu licebit agere. Quum enim de vno contrario in alterum contrarium fit transitus, non sine motu fit. Neque motus de vno in alterum intelligitur absque contrarietate quadam. Explicandum fuisse quot modis dicatur contrarium, ex eo intelligitur, quod categoriarum generibus quibusdam contrarietas accidat. Neque solum rerum Physicarum, verumetiam logicarum propositionum, adeóque differentiarum & ἑτεροῦ⁠ν habita ratione, notitia contrarietatis est necessaria Dialectico. In categoriarum etiam generibus prius & posterius habet locum. Prior enim est substantia accidentibus: prima etiam substantia, ac secunda dicitur. In Relatis prior est mensura ipso mensurato. Et vt quæ priora, quæ posteriora: ita etiā quæ simul sunt, nolle par est. Motus neque absq; contrariis, neque absque priore & posteriore intelligi potest. Quantitates ποσότητος: categoriæ actionis & passionis, non possunt intelligi absq; motus aliqua notitia. Denique ipsum habere, quum sit homonymum multisque modis diuersis generibus categoriarū tribuatur, distinguendum fuit postremò. Dico postremò: nam Κατὰ γένος (quæ vt genera sternuntur his communibus accidentibus) postrema etiam fuit categoria τῆς ἔχειν.
units.tr: Those who wish the categories to be removed from Dialectic use also this argument: that the things after the categories (τὰ μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας) do not in any way pertain to the dialectician. For, they say, it is not the business of the dialectician to treat of opposites or of contraries, and much less of motion, whose consideration pertains to the natural philosopher. Since, therefore, by removing the things after the categories they wish the categories to be removed as well, (if it is permitted to posit the categories), then it will also be permitted to posit the things after the categories. And yet we have shown that the categories must be posited by the rule of "of everything" and "in itself." As for what they allege concerning motion, it is specious indeed, but nevertheless false: that the dialectician must in no way treat of motion in the categories. For if he may treat of contraries, he may also treat of motion. For when there is a transition from one contrary to the other contrary, it does not occur without motion; nor is motion understood from one thing to another without a certain contrariety. That the word "contrary" must be explained in how many ways it is said is understood from the fact that contrariety befalls certain genera of the categories. Nor is knowledge of contrariety necessary to the dialectician only with respect to physical things, but also with respect to logical propositions, and indeed with respect to differences and otherness (ἑτερότης). In the genera of the categories too, the prior and posterior have their place. For substance is prior to accidents; it is also called primary substance and secondary. In relatives, the measure is prior to the thing measured. And just as there are things which are prior and posterior, so it is also not proper to deny that there are things which are simultaneous. Motion can be understood neither without contraries nor without a prior and a posterior. The quantities of quantity (ποσότητος), and the categories of action and passion, cannot be understood without some knowledge of motion. Finally, since "to have" is homonymous and is attributed in many diverse ways to the genera of the categories, it had to be distinguished last. I say last: for the category of "having" was also the last, according to genus (κατὰ γένος), which is laid out by these common accidents as genera.

units.la: Περὶ ἀντικειμένων, seu de oppositis.
units.tr: On opposites (Περὶ ἀντικειμένων), or on opposites.

units.la: Ἀντικείμενα opposita, vel aduersantia, vel pugnantia dici possunt. Ac ἀντίθεσις seu oppositio inter duo est, quæ in eodem simul eadem ratione inesse nequeunt. Quatuor autem sunt genera ἀντικειμένων: Relata, contraria, priuantia, contradicentia.
units.tr: Opposites (ἀντικείμενα) may be called opposed, or adverse, or conflicting. And opposition (ἀντίθεσις) is between two things which cannot be present together in the same thing at the same time in the same respect. There are four genera of opposites: relatives, contraries, privatives, and contradictories.

units.la: Relatorum vnum vni sic opponitur,vt totum ipsius esse,ratione oppositi,quod correlatum vnò[?] cant[?],intelligatur. Cum igitur vnum sine altero definiri nō possit, præ cæteris oppositis arctissimè iuncta esse relata iudicabuntur. Adhæc ex oppositis sola relata propter arctissimam necessitatem (ob quam vnum alterum subinfert) cate-goriæ genus peculiare constituunt.
units.tr: Of relatives, one is opposed to another in such a way that the being of the one is understood in relation to the other, which is called its correlate. Since therefore one cannot be defined without the other, relatives will be judged to be joined more closely than the other opposites. Moreover, of opposites, relatives alone, on account of their very close necessity (by which one infers the other), constitute a peculiar genus of the category.

units.la: Reliqua verò opposita suam quaeque categoriam non constituunt, sed susa[?] sunt per categorias. Sunt autem tria genera relatorum, de quibus in categoria τῶν πρός τι.
units.tr: But the remaining opposites do not each constitute a category of their own, but are distributed among the categories. There are, however, three genera of relatives, which are discussed in the category of relatives (τῶν πρός τι).

units.la: Contraria sunt quæ sub eodem genere posi-ta longissimo interuallo distant inter se, & se mutuò de subiecto expellunt. Horum non potest esse peculiaris aliqua categoria, vt Relatorum: quia oppositum contrarium perimit essentiam alterius oppositi,non autem constituit. Ad hæc contrarietas non in vna categoria locum habet.
units.tr: Contraries are those which, placed under the same genus, are separated from each other by the greatest interval, and mutually expel each other from the subject. Of these there cannot be any peculiar category, as there is for relatives; because one contrary destroys the essence of the other opposite, but does not constitute it. Moreover, contrariety does not have its place in only one category.

units.la: Prima autem contraria sunt ἕξις & στέρησις. Omnis enim differentia habitu & priuatione requadā describitur ἐν γένει, seu sub genere. & est species[?] veluti affirmatio & negatio ἄμεσος. Quæ eo di cuntur vt ostendatur communio quædam generum horum oppositorum: quorū discrimen posthea notabitur. Quod si quis dicat esse differentias μεταξύ inter primam summi generis differentiam, & vltimam εἰδοποιόν: respondemus differentias illas, quæ sunt μεταξύ, nō opponi contrariè, habita ratione differentiæ εἰδοποιῶς: sed ratione generis contrariè opponi affirmamus: quia diuidunt genus ἀμέσως. Denique omnia contraria sunt aut ἐξις καὶ στέρησις, aut ἕξει καὶ στερήσει participant: ieu non omnis ἕξις καὶ στέρησις contrariè opponuntur: vt dicemus paulò post.
units.tr: The first contraries, however, are habit (ἕξις) and privation (στέρησις). For every difference is described in some way by habit and privation within a genus (ἐν γένει), or under a genus; and affirmation and negation are, as it were, immediate. These are said so that a certain commonality of these opposed genera may be shown, whose distinction will be noted afterwards. But if someone says that there are differences intermediate between the first difference of the highest genus and the last specific difference (εἰδοποιόν), we reply that those differences which are intermediate are not opposed as contraries, considered with respect to the specific difference; but we affirm that they are opposed as contraries with respect to the genus, because they divide the genus immediately. Finally, all contraries are either habit and privation, or they share in habit and privation; that is, not every habit and privation is opposed as contraries, as we shall say a little later.

units.la: Contraria etiam ratione subiecti dicuntur illa, quorum mobile subiectum est inst-ar materiæ mutabilis, contrariis obnoxiæ. Quæ genus lo-cum habent, ratione suorum πρώτων δεκτικῶν (eu subiecto-um, sunt etiam consideranda. Neque enim generis consideratio in contrariis excludit considerationem subiecti. Horum con-trariorum quædam habent aliquid μεταξύ: quæ-dam non habent. Contrariorum accidentium est medium, nempe illorum, quorum causa ἀεὶ ἃ sunt mobiles. Fit enim transitus ab uno extremo ad alterum per media. Sic non omne coloratum est album aut nigrum: potest enim esse viride, aut puniceum. Quædam sunt contraria, quæ ratione habituum, aut generis, nullum habent ἀ-νάμεσον. Si omnis habitu ethico prædicus necessario iustus est: aut iniustus ratione generis habitus. At ratione subiecti πεφυκὸς, potest aliquis describi priuatione iusti, & iniusti vt puer qui nondum sit iustus aut iniustus: & tamen sit πεφυκὼς, vt possit esse iustus aut iniustus. In Theologia nihil est μεταξύ inter iustum & iniustum. Nam ratione originis nostræ, ἀμέσως omnis iustus est, aut iniustus. In quibusdam ipsum τὸ μεταξύ est ἀνώνυμον. In aliis τὸ μεταξύ nominatū estsic illud,quod neq; maius neq; minus est,æquale dicitur. Nullū aūt intercedit mediū, quando respectu generis contraria ipsa oppo-nuntur : sic animatum omne sanum aut ægrum ἀμέσως, respectu generis,dicitur. Sic habitus ipsi tanquam fines,misceri & confundi nequeūt, eo modo quo album & nigrum miscentur in in-termediis coloribus.
units.tr: Things are also called contraries with respect to the subject, those whose mobile subject is like the matter that is mutable and liable to the contraries. These have a place in the genus, with respect to their first receptive subjects (or subjects), and are also to be considered. For the consideration of the genus among contraries does not exclude the consideration of the subject. Of these contraries, some have something intermediate, and some do not. Of contrary accidents there is a middle, namely of those whose cause is that they are always mobile. For transition is made from one extreme to the other through the intermediates. Thus not every colored thing is white or black; for it can be green or purple. Some contraries, with respect to habits or genus, have no intermediate at all. If every person endowed with an ethical habit is necessarily just or unjust by the habit's genus. But with respect to the subject that is naturally fitted (πεφυκὸς), someone can be described by the privation of justice and injustice, like a boy who is not yet just or unjust, and yet is naturally fitted to be able to be just or unjust. In theology there is nothing intermediate between the just and the unjust. For by reason of our origin, every person is immediately either just or unjust. In some cases the intermediate itself is nameless. In others the intermediate is named: that which is neither greater nor less is said to be equal. Moreover no intermediate lies between when the contraries are opposed themselves with respect to the genus: thus every living thing is said to be healthy or sick immediately, with respect to the genus. So also habits themselves, as extremes, cannot be mixed and blended, in the way that white and black are mixed in intermediate colors.

units.la: Priuantia quæ opponuntur vt στέρησις & ἕξις, non eodem genere(vt contraria) sed eodem subiecto participant. Ac priuatio quidem hic,quum nullius generis fit particeps, species non poterit esse, sed erit duntaxat τῇ εἴδει[?] negatio συνειλημμένη τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ[?]. Priuatio igi-tur negatione formæ, quæ subiecto quodam certo determinata sit,intelligitur. Est enim ἀ-πουσία τῆς εἴδους ἐν τῷ περιέχοντι[?]. Est autem pri-uatio τῶν πολλαχῶς λεγομένων. Primò enim significat ἀπουσίαν τῆς εἴδους, absentiam formæ constituentis speciem. Sic in Physicis priuatio dicitur absentia formæ in materia. Secundò si- gnificat priuationem non ἕξεως, sed σχέσεως. Sic tenebræ dicuntur priuatio luminis. Sic actionis & passionis priuatio est quies: actio vero & passio non sunt ἕκτικὸν[?], sed σχετικόν quiddam. Tertiò priuatio respectu generis dicitur: vt cum differētia differentiæ opponitur sub eodem genere. De hac priuatione in contrariis dictum est.
units.tr: Privative opposites, such as privation and habit (στέρησις and ἕξις), do not share a genus as contraries do, but they share a subject. A privation, since it belongs to no genus, cannot be a species; it is merely a negation of a form (τῇ εἴδει[?]) conjoined with the subject (τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ[?]). A privation is therefore understood as the negation of a form that is determined by some definite subject. For it is the absence of the form (ἀ-πουσία τῆς εἴδους ἐν τῷ περιέχοντι[?]). Privation, however, is said in several ways (τῶν πολλαχῶς λεγομένων). First, it signifies the absence of the form, the absence of the form constituting the species. Thus in the natural sciences, privation is called the absence of form in matter. Secondly, it signifies the privation not of a habit but of a relation (σχέσεως). Thus darkness is called the privation of light. So too the privation of action and passion is rest; action and passion, however, are not a habit (ἕκτικὸν[?]) but something relative (σχετικόν). Thirdly, privation is said with respect to a genus, as when one difference is opposed to another difference under the same genus. Of this kind of privation we have spoken among the contraries.

units.la: Omnium autem priuationum perfectissima est illa, quibus negatur ἐν τοῖς ἑκτικοῖς[?] solùm παρουσία εἶδος, verumetiā ipsa δύναμις πα-ρουσίας. Huius igitur perfectissimae priuationis tres sunt conditiones. Prima conditio est: nega-tio nō solum habitus, verumetiam δυνάμεως. Secunda, in subiecto πεφυκότι. Tertia, in tem-pore illo, quo subiectum πεφυκὸς praeditum ef-fe solet habitu ipso. Sic edentulum esse, non est simpliciter, non habere dentes, sed quando habere oportet, non habere.
units.tr: Yet the most perfect of all privations is that in which there is denied, in the things that are capable (ἐν τοῖς ἑκτικοῖς[?]), not only the presence of the form but also the very capacity (δύναμις) for its presence. There are, therefore, three conditions of this most perfect privation. The first condition is: the negation not only of the habit but also of the capacity. The second: in a subject that is naturally fitted (πεφυκότι) for it. The third: at that time when the naturally fitted subject is wont to be endowed with the habit itself. Thus to be toothless is not simply to have no teeth, but to lack them when one ought to have them.

units.la: Cæterum quanuis videns & cæcū animal opponantur, vt ἕξις & στέρησις: tamē discrimen est inter priuationē & rem priuatam. Priuatio.n.nō accidit oculo per se secundo modo τῷ καθ' αὑτό[?]. Si enim oculo accideret per se secundo modo, cæcitas non perimeret essentiam oculi: at perimit. Deinde oculus posset dici cæcus: at non potest dici cæcus. Animali vero oculato per se quarto modo accidit priuatio illa visus: qua ratione animal cæcum, non oculus cæcus, dicitur.
units.tr: Moreover, although a seeing animal and a blind animal are opposed as habit and privation, there is nevertheless a difference between a privation and a privated thing. For privation does not befall the eye per se in the second way (τῷ καθ' αὑτό[?]). If it befell the eye per se in the second way, blindness would destroy the essence of the eye; but it does destroy it. Again, the eye could be called blind; but it cannot be called blind. Privation, however, befalls a sighted animal per se in the fourth way; and for this reason the animal, not the eye, is called blind.

units.la: Quartum genus oppositionis est, vt affirma-tio & negatio. Neque vero res affirmata aut ne-gata est ipsa affirmatio aut negatio (nam res af-firmata aut negata extra mentem est) verum op-ponitur vt affirmatio aut negatio. Cæterum hæc oppositio nullo tertio limitatur, neque ge-nere neque subiecto: vt in contrariis & priuanti-bus vsu venit: estque primum lumen intellectus, quo rē esse aut non esse pronunciamus. vt quid-quid est, aut est homo, aut non est homo: aut in-cedit aut non incedit. ἀνάγκη δὲ ἢ φάναι ἢ ἀπο-φάναι.
units.tr: The fourth kind of opposition is that of affirmation and negation. Now a thing affirmed or denied is not itself the affirmation or negation (for a thing affirmed or denied exists outside the mind), but these are opposed as affirmation and negation. Moreover, this opposition is limited by no third term, neither by genus nor by subject, as happens with contraries and privatives. It is the first principle of the intellect, by which we pronounce that a thing is or is not: for example, whatever exists, either is a man or is not a man; either walks or does not walk. Necessity demands either to affirm or to deny (ἀνάγκη δὲ ἢ φάναι ἢ ἀπο-φάναι).

units.la: Hæc autem quatuor genera τῶν ἀντικειμέ-νων hunc in[?] modum discernuntur.
units.tr: These four kinds of opposites (τῶν ἀντικειμέ-νων) are distinguished in the following manner.

units.la: Quæ opponuntur vt ἕξις & στέρησις non sunt τῶν πρός τι. Quanuis, n. priuatio sine habitu nō intelligitur: tamen priuatio, nō dicitur quidquid θέσιν ἕξ[?] est, id ipsum esse habitus: quo modo duplum id, ipsum quod est, dimidii duplum est. Imò priuatio simul esse eum habitu nequit. *Præ-terea quæ vt ἕξις & στέρησις opponuntur, à contrariis differunt, siue sint ἀμέσα, siue ἐμμέσα contraria. Quod ad ἀμέσα contraria attinet, alterutrum inest necessario. Vt omne animatum est sanum aut ægrum: omnis numerus est par aut impar. (Differētiæ enim in contrariis numeran-tur) At in priuantibus potest esse subiectū, quod nondum habitu sit præditum, sed possit esse: vt quod nōdum iustum est aut iniustum: sed tamen est capax iustitiæ aut iniustitiæ, vt supra dixi-mus. Priuantia verò differunt à contrariis illis, quæ ἐμμέσα dicuntur, seu quæ ἀναμέσον habēt, eò quod contrariorum, quorum est aliquod μεταξύ, non necesse sit alterutrum inesse. neque e-nim necesse est certo aliquo tempore, aliquid frigidum aut calidum esse: potest enim esse tepi-dum quolibet tempore. At illorum quæ στερητικῶς opponuntur, ratione subiectorum proprio-rum δεκτικῶν, quo tempore fert natura, alterutrum necessario inest. Omne enim animal tum quum tempus est, aut videns, aut cæcum est. Neque alterutrum necessario inest, vt igni calor, aut niui candor: sed ὡς ἔτυχεν, aut videre au cæ-
units.tr: Those opposed as habit and privation are not among the relatives (τῶν πρός τι). For although privation is not understood without habit, nevertheless whatever is privation is not thereby the habit itself, just as the double of a half is not the same as that which is the double of the half. Indeed, privation cannot be together with habit at the same time. Furthermore, those opposed as habit and privation differ from contraries, whether they are immediate (ἀμέσα) or mediate (ἐμμέσα) contraries. As regards immediate contraries, one of the two necessarily inheres: for example, every animal is either healthy or sick; every number is either even or odd (for differences are counted among the contraries). But in privatives there may be a subject which has not yet been endowed with the habit, yet is capable of it, as what is not yet just or unjust, but nevertheless is capable of justice or injustice, as I said above. Privatives, however, differ from those contraries called mediate, or which have an intermediate, because of contraries of which one has an intermediate, it is not necessary that one of the two inhere. For it is not necessary that at a certain time something be either cold or hot; for it can be lukewarm at any time. But of those opposed by privation, with respect to their proper receptive subjects, one of the two necessarily inheres at the time when nature brings it forth. For every animal, when the time comes, is either seeing or blind. Yet with respect to fire, heat, or with respect to snow, whiteness, neither of the two necessarily inheres, but as it happens, either seeing or blind inheres.

units.la: cum esse inest. Ad hæc contraria pleraque sunt permutabilia inter se: exceptis illis, quæ ex na-turali & immutabili principio insunt: quo mo-do insunt igni calor, & niui albedo: quæ tamen aliis subiectis ita insunt, vt permutari contrariis possint. Quod & in habitibus contrariis vsuue-nit. Ex bonis enim plerunque improbi fiunt ho-mines: & ex improbis boni. At habitus priua-tione quidem commutari potest: sed non vicis-situdine per sim priuatio habitu commutatur. Nam quæ ve- dicitur priuatio: non solùm actum verume-tiam δύναμιν τὴν [?]περιχότος perimit. Eiusmodi est στερητικὴ ἀντίθεσις, in qua considerantur tria: primò subiectum, quod est οὐσία naturalis: secundò, subiecti φύσις, quæ est principium [?]ἕξεως: tertiò, negatio ἕξεως includens στέρησιν. Φασιν δύναμεως. *Affirmatio verò & negatio (quæ prima & simplicissima est ἀντίθεσις ratio-ne subiecti eiusdem) discernitur ab aliis generi- bus oppositorum, eò quòd alia opposita, non sem per nec in omnibus, siue simpliciter siue complexè proferantur, verum & falsum distinguunt. Alia non oppositá limitantur vel genere, vel subiecto ἀντίθεσις: ac neutrum oppositorum illorum est verum, sed utrumque falsum, si dicantur de illis quæ sunt extra limitantia vel genera vel subiecta. Sic extra animatum corpus, nihil sanum neque ægrum vere dicitur. In priuantibus, extra perfectum animal & ἀπέρ[?]ος, nihil videns aut cæcum dicitur. Extra quantitatem vel relatio-nem, neque duplum neque dimidium intelligi-tur. tur.At affirmatio & negatio, semper & in omni- bus generibus verum & falsum diuidunt absque vlla determinatione vel generis, vel subiecti τῆς φυκότος[?], vel temporis. Ad hæc contrariorum ἀμέσων alterutrum necessariò non inest, alia ra- tione, quàm quatenus prædicantur de subiecto, vel temporis causa. Sic ἔνεκα λόγου κα- θόλως, de animato dicitur sanum & ægrum. Tem poris causa de Socrate, aut Platone. Nam qua- tenus Socrates est, verum est dicere Socratem esse sanum aut ægrum. Quod si non sit Socrates, utrunque falsum est. Quod etiam in priuantibus habet locum. Quatenus enim non est Socrates, neque videns neque cæcus dici poterit. At illa quæ sunt opposita, vt affirmatio & negatio, diui-dunt verum & falsum, per omnia, in omnibus, & semper: siue res sit siue non sit.
units.tr: With regard to these contraries, most are mutually changeable, except those which inhere by a natural and unchangeable principle, as heat inheres in fire and whiteness in snow; these nevertheless inhere in other subjects in such a way that they can be exchanged for their contraries. This also happens in contrary habits: for good men for the most part become wicked, and wicked men become good. But a habit can be changed by privation, yet privation is not changed into habit by mutual succession. For what is called privation destroys not only the act but also the capacity (δύναμιν τὴν [?]περιχότος). Such is privative opposition, in which three things are considered: first, the subject, which is a natural substance; secondly, the nature of the subject, which is the principle of the habit; thirdly, the negation of the habit, which includes privation. They say (Φασιν) of capacity. Affirmation and negation, however (which is the first and simplest opposition with respect to the same subject), are distinguished from the other kinds of opposites in that the other opposites do not always, nor in all cases, whether stated simply or in combination, distinguish true from false. Other opposites are limited either by genus or by subject; and neither of those opposites is true, but both are false, if they are said of things lying outside the limiting genera or subjects. Thus outside an animate body nothing is truly said to be healthy or sick. Among privatives, outside a perfect animal and one that is capable (ἀπέρ[?]ος), nothing is said to be seeing or blind. Outside quantity or relation, neither double nor half is understood. But affirmation and negation always and in all genera divide true from false, without any determination either of genus, or of subject, or of time. Moreover, of immediate contraries one does not necessarily inhere, except insofar as they are predicated of a subject, or for reasons of time. Thus, for the sake of general discourse, healthy and sick are said of an animate being; for the sake of time, of Socrates or Plato. For insofar as he is Socrates, it is true to say that Socrates is healthy or sick. But if he is not Socrates, both are false. This also holds for privatives: insofar as he is not Socrates, neither seeing nor blind can be said of him. But opposites such as affirmation and negation divide true from false in all respects, in all things, and always: whether the thing is or is not.

units.la: Contrariorum separata consideratio ex ratione boni & mali.
units.tr: The separate consideration of contraries from the standpoint of good and evil.

units.la: Quàm late pateat contrarietas, ex eo etiam intelligitur, quòd cótrariorum rationes, nisi sub ratione boni & mali (quæ duo genera sunt con- traria omnium amplissima) satis intelligi non possint. Cùm autem in categoriis tam sæpe fa-cta sit mentio contrariorum, & propter res, in notionibus simplicibus, & deinde in propositionibus contrarietas consideretur: operæpretium facturi videmur, si quàm latissimè se proferunt, id est, sub ratione boni & mali, contraria separa-tim consideremus. Amplissima hæc contraria nempe bonum & malū rebus propter materiam seu δυνάμιν [?] ἀντιφατικῶς [?] accidunt. Ac bonum quidem κατὰ φύσιν [?] dicitur: malum vero παρὰ φύσιν. Cúmq; vitiū, (quod ad malum κατὰ τὸ παρὰ φύσιν refertur) non solum virtuti sed & vitio opposito sit contrarium: videtur non vnum vni dun taxat, sed vnum pluribus posse esse contrarium. Sic enim iniustitia non solum cum iustitia contrariè pugnat, verum etiam iniustitia cum iniustitia. Quaedam enim iniustitia est, quae plus aequo dat: altera quae minus quam quod aequum est. Quare vt nihil quod pertineat ad contrariorum notitiam, Dialectico vtilem, praetermittamus: sciendum est, quaedam esse contraria, quae non solum vni, sed & pluribus contrariè opponantur: quorum ἀντίθεσις [?] contraria, quomodo distinguenda sit, exemplo virtutis & vitii declarabimus. Virtus vitio huic est contrariè opposita, ratione habitus moralis tàquam generis. Sic vitium vnum alteri contrariè opponitur ratione generis: vt prodigalitati, auaritia. Praeterea species virtutum, speciebus vitiorum sunt contrariae propter genera, quae sub genere qualitatis continentur. Quod autem vitium non solum virtuti, verum etiam vitio alteri contrario opponitur, in causa est virtutis definitio, quae constat συμπάθεια [?] duorum extremorum: vt enim aequale definitur συμπάθεια [?] maioris & minoris: ita mediocre intelligitur συμπάθεια [?] vtriusque ἀμετρίας [?]. Quanuis autem συμπάθεια [?] haec videatur esse ἔρησις [?]: tamen non est perfecta ἔρησις [?]. Virtus enim quae est mediocritas. tas, magis habet rationem ἕξεως καὶ ἕξις, quā στέρησις. Quare etiam dicitur contrarie opponi vitio, non vt στέρησις per se facta, cum vitium potius habeat rationem στερήσεως, quia malum est. Huiusmodi cōcursus contrariarum oppositionum in quibusdam cernitur, vt in virtutibus & vitiis. Item in habitibus firmæ valetudinis, & infirmæ. Morbi enim sunt inter se contrarii: & quælibet species sanitatis tāquam συμμετρία, morbis contrarie opponitur. Exuperās quidem & exuperatum relatē opponuntur: at respectu medii, quod definitur σωματοφθορεῖ exuperantis & exuperati, contrarie opponuntur.
units.tr: How widely contrariety extends can also be understood from this: the reasons for contraries cannot be sufficiently understood except under the aspect of good and evil, which are the two most comprehensive kinds of contraries. Since, however, mention of contraries is made so often in the Categories, and contrariety is considered both among the things in simple notions and then in propositions, we shall seem to be doing a worthwhile task if we consider contraries separately under the aspect of good and evil, that is, in the broadest sense in which they present themselves. These most comprehensive contraries, good and evil, accrue to things on account of matter or potency [?] antiphatikôs [?]. Good is said to be according to nature [kata physin]; evil, however, contrary to nature [para physin]. And since vice (which is referred to evil as "according to the contrary of nature") is contrary not only to virtue but also to the opposed vice, it seems that one thing can be contrary not only to one thing alone but to several things. For injustice not only fights contrariwise with justice, but also injustice with injustice. For there is one injustice which gives more than what is equal, and another which gives less than what is equal. Therefore, that we may omit nothing useful to the dialectician that pertains to the knowledge of contraries, it must be understood that some contraries are opposed contrariwise not only to one thing but also to several; the opposition [antithesis] of these, how they are to be distinguished, we shall make clear by the example of virtue and vice. Virtue is contrariwise opposed to this vice, in respect of moral habit as genus. Thus one vice is contrariwise opposed to another in respect of genus, as prodigality to avarice. Besides, the species of virtues are contrary to the species of vices on account of the genera which are contained under the genus of quality. Now, that a vice is opposed not only to virtue but also to another contrary vice has its cause in the definition of virtue, which consists in a symmetry [sympatheia] of two extremes: for just as the equal is defined as a symmetry [sympatheia] of the greater and the less, so the mean is understood as a symmetry [sympatheia] of each excess [ametria]. Although, however, this symmetry [sympatheia] seems to be a privation [hairesis], yet it is not a perfect privation. For virtue, which is mediocrity, has more the character of a habit and a having [hexis kai hexis] than of a privation [sterêsis]. Therefore it is also said to be contrariwise opposed to vice, not as a privation considered in itself, since vice rather has the character of a privation because it is an evil. Such a concurrence of contrary oppositions is seen in certain things, as in virtues and vices; likewise in the habits of firm health and of weak health. For diseases are contrary to one another, and any species of health, as a symmetry [symmetria], is contrariwise opposed to diseases. Excess and the thing exceeded are opposed relatively; but with respect to the mean, which is defined as the corruption [sômatophthorei] of the excess and the thing exceeded, they are opposed contrariwise.

units.la: Ac plerunque contrarium vnum vni opponitur, vt bonum malo. Sic differentiæ vltimæ inter se opponuntur, sub ratione priuationis cuiusdam. Item contraria accidentia siue ἄυεσα siue ἐμμεσα sub ratione boni & mali, id est, habitus & priuationis cuiusdam, opponuntur: vt calidum frigido, album nigro.
units.tr: And for the most part one contrary is opposed to one, as good to evil. Thus the last differences are opposed to one another under the aspect of a certain privation. Likewise contrary accidents, whether proper [per se] or by means [per accidens], are opposed under the aspect of good and evil, that is, of a habit and of a certain privation: as hot to cold, white to black.

units.la: Cum autem bonum in contrariis, ἕξεως ratione habeat: erit quoque instar mensuræ & est principii: & quia mensura est bonum, prius erit instar suo mensurato. Neque si vnum fuerit, necessario etiam alterum erit: bonum enim potest esse, etiamsi malum nullum sit: & habitus potest esse, etiamsi nulla sit priuatio. Quare quandoque contraria sub ratione boni & mali intelliguntur: si vnum sit, non erit necesse alterum esse. Natura non esse simul contraria, probat Aristoteles hunc in modum: sanis omnibus existentibus, sanitas potest esse nullo existente morbo: & fi alba sint omnia, albedo absque nigredine existet. Quod indicimus, in diuiduis repoi is causa magis perspicuum est: Socrates enim idem fanus & ægrotus esse nequit. Quare contraria simul esse nequeunt.
units.tr: Since, however, the good among contraries has the character of a habit, it will also be like a measure and of a principle; and because the measure is a good, it will be prior, like what is measured by it. Nor, if one of them exists, will the other necessarily exist as well: for a good can exist even if no evil exists, and a habit can exist even if there is no privation. Therefore, sometimes contraries are understood under the aspect of good and evil: if one exists, it is not necessary for the other to exist. Aristotle proves in this manner that contraries are not by nature simultaneous: with all things being healthy, health can exist when no disease exists; and if all things are white, whiteness will exist without blackness. What we point out is more evident in individuals, for the reason: Socrates cannot be both healthy and sick at the same time. Therefore contraries cannot be simultaneous.

units.la: Præterea notandum est contraria esse aut sub genere quodam, aut circa subiectum quoddam, ex quo mutuo sese depellunt, aut esse ipsa genera. Ariftoteles hoc in loco εἶδος, πρῶτον δικαιον appellat. Neque solùm sub quo genere contraria sint considerandum est: verum etiā quod-cafubie nam fit πρῶτον δικαιικόν. Iustitia & iniustitia dicuntur in homine inesse tanquam in subiecto, sunt sed non fatis distinctè: diftinctius, fi in anima: di-pfa ftinctiffimè, fi in parte appetente, vt ἐν πρώτῳ δικαιῳ inesse cognoscantur. Quædam contrarie opponuntur causa generum contrariorum: vt iustitia & iniustitia, quæ sub contrariis sunt generibus, nempe virtute & vitio. Quædam opponuntur contrarié tanquam species, quæ genus idem habeant: vt album & nigrum: sunt enim species coloris. At bonum & malum opposita sunt & contraria, tanquam generalia quædam, vt quæ in omni genere contrariorum reperiantur.
units.tr: Moreover, it must be noted that contraries are either under some genus, or about some subject, by which they mutually drive each other away, or are themselves genera. Aristotle calls this in this place "species, first justice." Nor is it only necessary to consider under what genus the contraries are; but also in what subject they are, which is called the first subject. Justice and injustice are said to be in man as in a subject; but this is not sufficiently distinct: it is more distinct if they are said to be in the soul, and most distinctly if in the appetitive part, so that they are known to be in the first justice [en prōtō dikaiō]. Some are contrariwise opposed on account of contrary genera: as justice and injustice, which are under contrary genera, namely virtue and vice. Some are opposed contrariwise as species which have the same genus: as white and black; for they are species of colour. But good and evil are opposed and contrary as certain most general things, as those which are found in every genus of contraries.

units.la: Περὶ πρότερου de modis Prioris.
units.tr: On the Modes of "Prior" (Περὶ πρότερου): On the Modes of Prior.

units.la: Prius aliquid aliquo dicitur in contrariis: vt bonū malo prius est. & in distinctione partium motus: nam partes motionis, causa temporis diftinguntur fecundùm prius & posterius: & in relatis: vt, mensura prior est mensurato. Denique in multis rationibus consideratur τὸ πρότερον[?]. quo fit vt quot modis dicatur πρότερον post explicationem categoriarum, paucis completi sit necessarium, vt nihil praetermittatur eorū, quae categorias consequuntur.
units.tr: Something is said to be prior to something in the case of contraries, as good is prior to evil. It is also used in the distinction of the parts of motion: for the parts of a motion are distinguished according to prior and posterior by reason of time. And it is used of relatives: thus the measure is prior to the thing measured. Finally, the notion of what is prior (τὸ πρότερον) is considered in many arguments. Hence, since the explanation of the categories is complete, it is necessary to set out briefly how many modes of "prior" there are, so that nothing is passed over of those things which follow from the categories.

units.la: Primus modus prioris est, quo prius aliquid causa[?] temporis dicitur. Sic antiquiora priora sunt recentioribus. Et prius puer aut adolescens est aliquis, quàm senex. Hic primus modus prioris est κυριώτατος[?]: quia consideratur ἐν τοῖς καθ-ἕκαστα, quae maximè & praecipuè dicuntur esse, vt de primis substantiis dictum est. Tempore autem prius & γενέσει prius non differunt.
units.tr: The first mode of prior is that by which something is said to be prior by reason of time. Thus older things are prior to more recent things, and someone who is a boy or a youth is prior to someone who is an old man. This first mode of prior is the most proper (κυριώτατος), because it is considered in individual things (ἐν τοῖς καθ᾽ ἕκαστα), which are said most of all and chiefly to be, as was said of the primary substances. Yet what is prior in time and what is prior in generation (γενέσει) do not differ.
