units.la: Secundus modus est: cùm aliquid sic est, vt non necesse sit, posterius esse: sed contrà posteriore posito, necesse sit illud alterum esse. Sic triangulus dicitur prius in polygoniis: quia mensura est polygoniorum. Denique idem est dicere prius aliquid esse φύσει, εἴδει, οὐσίᾳ[?].
units.tr: The second mode is this: when one thing is such that it is not necessary for the other to be posterior, but, on the contrary, once the posterior is posited, it is necessary that the other be. Thus the triangle is said to be prior in relation to polygons, because it is the measure of polygons. Finally, to say that something is prior by nature (φύσει), by kind (εἴδει), or in substance (οὐσίᾳ) is the same thing.

units.la: Caeterùm non quicquid est prius λόγῳ illud etiam prius est φύσει. multitudo prior est vnitate, τῷ λόγῳ quia vnitas absque mentione multitudinis definiri nō potest. Est enim vnitas quae λόγῳ: diuidi in multa non potest. At vnitas tamen φύσει prior est. Quaedam etiam sunt simul λόγῳ, quorum vnum est altero prius φύσει. Mensura enim & mensuratum, quia relata, λόγῳ sunt simul: verùm φύσει mensura prior est.
units.tr: Moreover, not everything that is prior in reason (λόγῳ) is also prior by nature. Plurality is prior to unity in reason, because unity cannot be defined without mention of plurality. For unity is that which is one in reason: it cannot be divided into many. Yet unity is nonetheless prior by nature. Some things are also simultaneous in reason, of which one is prior to the other by nature. For the measure and the thing measured, being relatives, are simultaneous in reason; but by nature the measure is prior.

units.la: Quaedam verò sunt, vt τῷ λόγῳ, ita etiam φύσει φύσει priora. Sic ἐνέργεια respectu δυνάμεως & λόγῳ est prior φύσει & λόγῳ: prior φύσει, quia δύνα-μις[?] λόγῳ. μιᾷ[?] ἐστι propter ἐνέργειαν prior natura: quia τῷ δυνάμει ὂν non definitur alia ratione, quàm ratione ἐνεργείας: vt τὸ ὁρατικὸν definitur τῷ ὁρᾶν.
units.tr: Some things, however, are prior both in reason and likewise by nature. Thus actuality (ἐνέργεια) is prior to potentiality (δύναμις) both in reason and by nature: prior by nature, because the potential, which is in potency, is not defined in any other way than by reference to actuality; thus the faculty of seeing (τὸ ὁρατικόν) is defined by seeing (τῷ ὁρᾶν).

units.la: Περὶ τὰ ἅμα. De modis simul.
units.tr: On Things Simultaneous (Περὶ τὰ ἅμα): On the Modes of Simultaneous.

units.la: Quæ simul sunt, priuatione prioris & posterioris, de quibus diximus, noscuntur. Primus autem modus, quo dicuntur res esse simul, est: cum ratione γενέσεως dicuntur esse simul: vt quæ simul fiunt & desinunt fieri. Simul autem esse dicuntur causa temporis. In tempore esse dicuntur propter motionem & γένεσιν. Motus enim per se, & γενέσεις sunt in tempore. Cum autem quietis partes non mensurentur tempore, vt partes motionis, non dicentur quietis partes fieri & desinere simul.
units.tr: Things that are simultaneous are known by the privation of prior and posterior, of which we have spoken. The first mode by which things are said to be simultaneous is this: they are said to be simultaneous by reason of generation, as things that come into being together and cease to come into being together. Things are said to be simultaneous by reason of time, and to be in time on account of motion and generation: for motion as such and generations are in time. But since the parts of rest are not measured by time, as the parts of motion are, it is not said that the parts of rest begin and cease together.

units.la: Secundus modus est, quo τὰ ἀντιστρέφοντα dicuntur simul esse φύσει, nempe illa, quæ ratione definitionis inter se sunt reciproca: & q orū ἅμα. vnum non est alterius causa: cuiusmodi sunt relata primi & secundi generis, quæ quidquid sunt alterius esse dicuntur. Hæc simul φύσει esse dicuntur, ὅτι ἀντιστρέφει [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀκολουθεῖ.
units.tr: The second mode is that by which reciprocal things (τὰ ἀντιστρέφοντα) are said to be simultaneous by nature, namely those which are mutually reciprocal by definition, and of which neither is the cause of the other. Such are relatives of the first and second kind, which are said to be of one another whatever they are. These are said to be simultaneous by nature, because each reciprocates with the other and follows it.

units.la: Relata vero tertii generis: Item subiecta omnia & propria ἀντιστρέφοντα. Item αἰτίαι συνεκτικαὶ, earúmq; effecta: quanuis sint simul tempore: quæ simul sunt, tamen non sunt simul φύσει secundùm τὸ εἶ tempore, ἀντιστρέφει. Mensura enim potest definiri absque mentione mensurati, & causa absque mentione effectus. Item subiectum absque mentione προφύσει, prii ἀντιστρέφοντος.
units.tr: But relatives of the third kind are likewise reciprocal, and so are all subjects and properties. Likewise the causes that are mutually conjoined (αἰτίαι συνεκτικαί) and their effects, although they are simultaneous in time; and things that are simultaneous are nevertheless not simultaneous by nature in the sense of "being in time," which is reciprocal. For a measure can be defined without mention of the thing measured, and a cause without mention of its effect. Likewise a subject without mention of the property, which is reciprocal with it.

units.la: Tertius modus quo dicûtur quædam esse sì Termul: est ille quo species, aut differentiæ contra se mutuò distinctæ, simul esse dicuntur φύσει sic pennigerum, gradiens, natans, quia æque participant genere animalis, dicuntur esse simul φύσει. Vt autem differentiæ considerantur vt relata quædam (differentia enim respectu alterius est differentiæ, nec seipso aliquid est) τῷ λόγῳ simul esse dicuntur.
units.tr: The third mode by which some things are said to be simultaneous is that by which species, or differences mutually distinct from one another, are said to be simultaneous by nature. Thus "feathered," "walking," and "swimming" are, because they equally share in the genus of animal, said to be simultaneous by nature. Yet insofar as differences are considered as certain relatives (for a difference is a difference in relation to another difference, and is nothing in itself), they are said to be simultaneous in reason.

units.la: De Motu.
units.tr: On Motion.

units.la: Motus quoque numerandus est ἐν τοῖς μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας. Nam secundum plures categorias, moueri res dicuntur, & transitus à contrario vno in alterum cum motione fit. Prius quoque ac posterius in motione consideratur. Et cùm primæ substantiæ vt ὑποκείμενα con-siderentur à Dialectico, de quibus prædicentur secundæ substantiæ: & primæ quidem substantiæ sint ὑποκείμενα ἁπλᾶ contrariorum: si considerare licet contrarietatem accidentium, quatenus prædicantur παρωνύμως de substantiis: licebit etiā considerare discrimina motuum per quos transitur ab vno contrario in alterum. Quod si quis dicat motus considerationem esse φυσικώτερον: sciat ille primæ substantiæ considerationem esse ὡς φυσικώτατον: sciat etiam priorum notionum & categoriarum distinctionem niti rebus ipsis tanquam fundamentis. De motu igitur dicendum est, quatenus ex vsu Dialectico esse nouimus.
units.tr: Motion must also be treated in the books after the Categories (ἐν τοῖς μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας). For things are said to be moved according to several categories, and transition from one contrary to the other takes place with motion. Prior and posterior are also considered in motion. And since the primary substances are considered by the Dialectician as subjects (ὑποκείμενα), of which the secondary substances are predicated; and the primary substances are simple subjects of contraries (ὑποκείμενα ἁπλᾶ), if it is permitted to consider the contrariety of accidents insofar as they are predicated paronymously (παρωνύμως) of substances, it will also be permitted to consider the differences of motions by which one passes from one contrary to the other. But if anyone should say that the consideration of motion is more physical (φυσικώτερον), let him know that the consideration of primary substance is most physical (ὡς φυσικώτατον); let him know also that the distinction of the prior notions and categories rests upon the things themselves as its foundations. Therefore we must speak of motion insofar as we know it to be useful to the Dialectician.

units.la: Sunt autem motionum sex genera, generatio, corruptio in genere substantiæ:incrementū,de-mentū in genere quantitatis:alteratio in genere qualitatis: & secundum locum motus,in categoria ubi.
units.tr: There are six kinds of motions: generation and corruption in the category of substance; increase and decrease in the category of quantity; alteration in the category of quality; and motion according to place, in the category of where.

units.la: Discernuntur autem hæc genera motuum hunc in modum. Ac primum generatio & cor-ruptio ab incremento, decremento, & ab al-teratione discernitur eo quòd non necesse fit quidquid increscit, decrescit, aut alteratur, il-lud etiam generari aut corrumpi. Multa enim alterantur & augentur, quæ tamen non gene-rantur. Adolescit adolescens, & tamen non ge-neratur.
units.tr: These kinds of motion are distinguished in the following way. First, generation and corruption are distinguished from increase, decrease, and alteration by the fact that it is not necessary that whatever increases, decreases, or is altered is also generated or corrupted. For many things are altered and grow that are nonetheless not generated: a youth grows up, and yet is not generated.

units.la: Quod autem alteratio & incrementum di-stincta sint genera eo probatur, quòd quædam augeri possint, quæ tamen non alterentur. Sic tetragona augentur gnomonibus, non mutata forma tetragoni. Si quaternario quinarius cir-cumponatur,fit nouenarius: ac augetur quidem numerus,sed nō alteratur. Nam nouenarius est quadratus vt & quaternarius.
units.tr: That alteration and increase are distinct kinds is proved by the fact that some things can be increased without being altered. Thus squares are increased by gnomons without their form as squares being changed. If a five is placed around a four, a nine results; the number is indeed increased, but not altered, for the nine is square just as the four is.

units.la: Motus autem in loco differt à reliquis mo-tionibus,eò quòd motis loco corporibus,neque generari,neque augeri,neque minui, neque alte-rari quippiam necesse fit.
units.tr: Motion in place differs from the other motions in that, when bodies are moved in place, it is not necessary that anything be generated, increased, diminished, or altered.

units.la: Cæterùm motui opponitur motus & quies. Ac motui quidem opponitur quies ἡρεμικῶς[?]. At contrariè opponitur motus, qui est ex contrario in contrarium. Sic generationi opponi-tur corruptio: incrementum decremento: Sic alteratio ex albo in nigrum, alterationi, quæ est ex nigro in album, contrarie opponitur. Sic etiam motus sursum, motui, quo deorsum fertur aliquid, contrarie aducrfatur.
units.tr: Moreover, motion is opposed to motion and to rest. Rest is opposed to motion in the manner of privation. But motion that goes from one contrary to another is contrarily opposed. Thus corruption is opposed to generation, and decrease to increase. Likewise alteration from white to black is contrarily opposed to alteration from black to white. Likewise motion upward is contrarily opposed to motion by which something is carried downward.

units.la: Περὶ τῷ ἔχειν[?].
units.tr: Concerning having (Περὶ τῷ ἔχειν).

units.la: Vt categoriarum postrema est τὸ ἔχειν.Ita etiam τῶν μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας postremum est τὸ ἔχειν: & vt illud quod nullum locum in aliis categoriis habet, ad τὸ ἔχειν refertur: ita etiam ἐν τοῖς μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας quod neque est oppositum, neque ad motum refertur, neque prius aut posterius aliquo modo dici potest, ἔχειν aliquo modo dicendum est.
units.tr: As τὸ ἔχειν is the last of the categories, so too τὸ ἔχειν is the last of the things that come after the categories [τὰ μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας]; and just as that which has no place among the other categories is referred to τὸ ἔχειν, so too among the things that come after the categories, whatever is neither opposite, nor referred to motion, nor can be called prior or posterior in any way, must be said to be in some way "having" (ἔχειν).

units.la: Si praedicetur aliquid, quod per habere definiatur, illud, in categoria τῷ ἔχειν erit reponendum. Sic motio cum definitur per actionem & passionem, ad categoria mactionis & passionis refertur.
units.tr: If something is predicated which is defined by "to have," it must be placed in the category of having. Thus motion, when it is defined through action and passion, is referred to the categories of action and passion.

units.la: Quod si non vt genus separatum τὸ ἔχειν con sideremus, sed vt susum per omnes categorias, necessariò categorias sequetur.
units.tr: But if we consider τὸ ἔχειν not as a separate genus, but as something that runs through all the categories, it will necessarily follow the categories.

units.la: Atque hic satis est quot modis habere dicatur, exponere paucis: quia non vt categoria consideratur. Habere igitur aliquis dicitur, vel vt habitum, vel vt ἕξιν: vt habere scientiam. Item in aliis categoriis: vt habere magnitudinem bicubitalem. Medimuus quoque dicitur habere frumenta, vt locus rem locatam, vel vt mensura rem mensuratam. Totum etiam dicitur habere partem, aut in parte habere aliquis dicitur, vt in digito annulum.
units.tr: Here it is enough to set out briefly the ways in which one is said to have, since it is not considered as a category. One is said to have either as a habit or as a state (ἕξις), as to have knowledge; likewise in the other categories, as to have a two-cubit magnitude. A measure is also said to have grain, the place to have the thing placed in it, or the measure to have the thing measured. A whole is also said to have a part, or one is said to have something in a part, as a ring on a finger.

units.la: Dicimus etiam habere agrum, vel ædes. Abutimur verò voce τῷ ἔχειν, cùm dicimus habere vxorem. Rectius συνοικεῖν diceremus, seu in eadem esse domo: vt relatio quædam ταυτότη-τος loci intelligatur. Proinde danda opera est, vt non solùm in categoriis, verumetiam ἐν τοῖς μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας, proprie & sapienter vocabula vsurpemus. Atq; hæc de illis quæ categorias sequuntur.
units.tr: We also say to have a field or a house. But we misuse the word τὸ ἔχειν when we say to have a wife; we would more correctly say συνοικεῖν, or to be in the same house, so that a certain relation of sameness of place is understood. Therefore care must be taken to use words properly and wisely not only in the categories but also in the things that come after the categories. And so much for those things that follow the categories.
